John of Montfort (c. 1295–1345) was a [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) nobleman who claimed the [Duchy of Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Duchy_of_Brittany), initiating the Breton War of Succession upon the death of his half-brother, Duke John III, in 1341.\[1\] As the son of [Arthur II, Duke of Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Arthur_II,_Duke_of_Brittany), and Yolande [de](https://grokipedia.com/page/DE) [Dreux](https://grokipedia.com/page/Dreux), Countess of Montfort, he contested the rival claim advanced by Charles [de](https://grokipedia.com/page/DE) [Blois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blois), the nephew of John III's widow and a candidate backed by King [Philip VI of France](https://grokipedia.com/page/Philip_VI_of_France).\[1\]\[2\] Summoned to [Paris](https://grokipedia.com/page/Paris), Montfort was arrested and imprisoned by Philip VI, but he escaped, traveled to [England](https://grokipedia.com/page/England), and secured military aid from Edward III by doing homage for Brittany, thereby drawing the duchy into the [Hundred Years' War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hundred_Years'_War).\[1\] Landing in Brittany in 1342, he recaptured [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes) and other fortifications, though subsequent defeats led to his recapture at [Auray](https://grokipedia.com/page/Auray) in 1343 and re-imprisonment.\[1\] Montfort escaped once more in 1345, reasserting his presence in the conflict before dying later that year at [Vannes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Vannes).\[1\] His persistent campaign, continued vigorously by his wife [Joan of Flanders](https://grokipedia.com/page/Joanna_of_Flanders) and later his son John V, culminated in the Montfort line's victory at the [Battle of Auray](https://grokipedia.com/page/Battle_of_Auray) in 1364, establishing their rule over [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany).\[3\]

Early Life and Family
---------------------

### Birth and Parentage

John of Montfort was born in 1295, the only son of Arthur II, Duke of Brittany (1266–1312), and his second wife, Yolande de Dreux (died after 1327), who held the title Countess of Montfort-l'Amaury in her own right.\[1\]\[4\] Arthur II's first marriage to Beatrice of England had produced legitimate heirs, including John III, Duke of Brittany (1286–1341), making Montfort a half-brother to the duke whose death precipitated the Breton War of Succession.\[1\] Yolande's claim to Montfort derived from her mother, Beatrice de Montfort (died c. 1306), daughter and heiress of the prominent crusader lord John I de Montfort (died 1249), ensuring that John inherited the county upon his mother's death.\[5\] No precise location or date for his birth is recorded in contemporary sources, though it occurred during Arthur II's tenure as duke following his succession in 1305.\[4\]

### Marriage and Heirs

John of Montfort married Joanna of Flanders, daughter of Louis I, Count of Nevers, and his wife Joan, Countess of Rethel, at Chartres in March 1329.\[6\] Joanna, born around 1295, survived her husband and played a prominent role in defending his claims to Brittany after his death in 1345, earning the epithet "Jeanne la Flamme" for her military leadership.\[6\] The marriage produced two children: a son, John, born in 1339, who inherited his father's claim to the Duchy of Brittany and ruled as John V from 1364 until his death in 1399; and an unnamed daughter born around 1341 who died young.\[6\] These heirs were central to perpetuating the Montfort line's challenge against the rival Blois-Penthièvre faction in the Breton War of Succession, with the son ultimately securing English support to consolidate power.\[6\]

Legal Basis of the Claim
------------------------

### Succession Laws in Brittany

The [Duchy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Duchy) of [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany)'s succession customs, derived from unwritten [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) traditions rather than [Roman](https://grokipedia.com/page/Roman) or strict feudal codes, permitted [female](https://grokipedia.com/page/Female) [inheritance](https://grokipedia.com/page/Inheritance) of the ducal [title](https://grokipedia.com/page/Title) in the absence of [direct](https://grokipedia.com/page/Di-rect) [male](https://grokipedia.com/page/Male) heirs, setting it apart from the agnatic [primogeniture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Primogeniture) enforced in the Kingdom of [France](https://grokipedia.com/page/France) under Salic principles. This allowance enabled women to accede as duchesses, with the title typically vesting in their husbands as consorts or passing to [issue](https://grokipedia.com/page/Issue) through the [female](https://grokipedia.com/page/Female) line, as demonstrated by historical precedents where [collateral](https://grokipedia.com/page/Collateral) [female](https://grokipedia.com/page/Female) claims were recognized over distant males.\[2\]\[7\] Male preference remained a core element, prioritizing direct male descendants and, in collateral succession, nearer male kin over females of equal or closer degree, though half-blood relations introduced interpretive challenges not explicitly resolved by custom. Upon Duke John III's death without sons on April 30, 1341, this framework pitted his half-brother John of Montfort—son of Duke Arthur II's second marriage—against claims through John III's full niece Joanna of Penthièvre, daughter of his sister [Marie](https://grokipedia.com/page/Marie). Montfort's advocates contended that a male sibling, even half-blood, held precedence over a female niece due to gender hierarchy and blood proximity, while opponents emphasized John III's prior favoritism toward the Penthièvre line via grants and implicit designation.\[2\]\[7\]\[8\] The absence of codified rules amplified noble divisions, with estates often apportioned by the duke's testamentary intentions or [arbitration](https://grokipedia.com/page/Arbitration), but ultimate validation required homage to the French [king](https://grokipedia.com/page/King) as [overlord](https://grokipedia.com/page/Overlord), intertwining local [custom](https://grokipedia.com/page/Custom) with royal oversight. This ambiguity, lacking mechanisms like equal partition among siblings common in some [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) regions for lesser lands, fueled prolonged litigation and armed conflict, underscoring how customary flexibility prioritized dynastic continuity over rigid exclusion.\[2\]\[7\]

### John's Rights Versus Rival Claims

John of Montfort derived his claim to the [Duchy of Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Duchy_of_Brittany) from his mother, Beatrice of Brittany, who was a [daughter](https://grokipedia.com/page/Daughter) of [Duke](https://grokipedia.com/page/Duke) Arthur II (r. 1305–1312) and thus a sister of the childless John III (r. 1312–1341). As the only surviving male descendant in the direct line from Arthur II through Beatrice, Montfort positioned himself as the rightful heir, emphasizing a preference for male [succession](https://grokipedia.com/page/Succession) in line with customs applicable to [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) peerages, to which [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) belonged. He invoked biblical authority from Numbers 27:8–9, which prioritizes sons over daughters in [inheritance](https://grokipedia.com/page/Inheritance), and [Roman law](https://grokipedia.com/page/Roman_law) precedents (e.g., Digest 38.10) prohibiting female transmission of certain estates, arguing these aligned with divine and feudal principles requiring male heirs for ducal sovereignty.\[2\] In opposition, the rival claimants were Joan of Penthièvre and her husband, Charles of Blois. Joan was the granddaughter of Arthur II through his daughter Joan of Brittany (another sister of John III), who had married into the Penthièvre family; this made Joan a first [cousin](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cousin) once removed to Montfort. The Penthièvre-Blois faction asserted that Breton customary law permitted inheritance through female representation, whereby a daughter could stand in place of her deceased father in the [succession](https://grokipedia.com/page/Succession) line, a practice supported by prior Breton entitlements and Joan's established inheritance of the Penthièvre counties. They contended that Joan's proximity in the female line—being only one generation removed from Arthur II's daughter—prevailed under local traditions that had historically allowed female ducal [succession](https://grokipedia.com/page/Succession) when male lines failed, contrasting Montfort's reliance on stricter French-influenced male-preference rules.\[2\] The dispute escalated to the [Parlement of Paris](https://grokipedia.com/page/Parlement_of_Paris), where Montfort initially sought recognition by offering homage to King Philip VI as overlord. However, on 7 September 1341, the court ruled in favor of Charles of [Blois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blois) and Joan of Penthièvre, affirming their claim based on Breton representational customs and dismissing Montfort's arguments for absolute male [primogeniture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Primogeniture). This decision reflected Philip VI's alignment with the Blois faction, to which he held kinship ties through Charles's Valois lineage, though it did not resolve underlying tensions over Brittany's semi-Salic traditions, which generally permitted female inheritance absent direct male heirs but prioritized male lines where possible. Montfort rejected the verdict, seizing [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes) on 10 September 1341 to assert control, thereby initiating armed conflict despite the legal adjudication.\[2\]

Outbreak of the Succession Crisis
---------------------------------

### Death of John III

[John III, Duke of Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany), died on **30 April 1341** at [Caen](https://grokipedia.com/page/Caen), having reached the age of 55 without producing any legitimate children from his three marriages.\[9\]\[3\] His passing left the duchy without a clear successor, igniting a protracted dynastic conflict rooted in competing interpretations of [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) [inheritance](https://grokipedia.com/page/Inheritance) customs, which favored male-preference [primogeniture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Primogeniture) in practice despite feudal complexities.\[10\] The immediate aftermath saw John of Montfort, John III's half-brother through their father Arthur II's second marriage, advance his claim based on proximity of blood and prior financial endowments from the duke, including 20,000 livres allocated shortly before the death.\[8\] Rival pretensions emanated from Joan of Penthièvre, John III's niece and goddaughter, whose husband Charles of Blois leveraged her designation in earlier ducal arrangements and support from King [Philip VI of France](https://grokipedia.com/page/Philip_VI_of_France), who viewed Montfort's assertion as a threat to Capetian influence.\[10\] Montfort moved decisively, seizing [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes) and procuring oaths of [fealty](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fealty) from local nobles, thereby proclaiming himself duke before French intervention could consolidate Blois's position.\[11\] This rapid escalation transformed the succession vacuum into open hostilities, drawing in English and French crowns amid the [Hundred Years' War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hundred_Years'_War) and entangling [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) in broader Anglo-French rivalries.\[12\]

### Initial Seizure of Power

Following the death of Duke John III on 30 April 1341 without direct male heirs, John of Montfort, his half-brother and a claimant by [proximity of blood](https://grokipedia.com/page/Proximity_of_blood), acted decisively to establish control over the [duchy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Duchy).\[13\] In May 1341, aided by a band of partisans, Montfort seized [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes), the administrative capital and a key stronghold, where he was proclaimed [duke](https://grokipedia.com/page/Duke) by an [assembly](https://grokipedia.com/page/Assembly) comprising deputies from the cities and lesser Breton nobility. The citizens of Nantes initially welcomed Montfort with enthusiasm, reflecting widespread urban and popular support for his claim amid resentment toward the perceived French influence favoring rival claimant Charles of Blois.\[14\] Montfort promptly secured the ducal treasury—likely including funds held at [Limoges](https://grokipedia.com/page/Limoges) earlier in the spring—and used these resources to consolidate authority, distributing patronage to secure loyalties among local lords and garrisons.\[13\] By midsummer 1341, Montfort had extended his hold to [Rennes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rennes) and other major centers, commanding the loyalty of approximately two-thirds of Brittany's fortified sites and leveraging the duchy's semi-autonomous traditions against centralized [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) arbitration.\[15\] This rapid power grab preceded the French royal court's formal judgment in [Paris](https://grokipedia.com/page/Paris), where the peers of [France](https://grokipedia.com/page/France) ultimately endorsed Charles of [Blois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blois) in September, prompting Montfort to defy the verdict and entrench his [de facto](https://grokipedia.com/page/De_facto) rule through [military occupation](https://grokipedia.com/page/Military_occupation).\[16\]

Phases of the Breton War of Succession
--------------------------------------

### Early Engagements and Capture (1341)

Following the death of his half-brother John III on 30 April 1341, John of Montfort hastened to [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes), the ducal capital, where he secured recognition as duke from an assembly of townsfolk and lesser [noble](https://grokipedia.com/page/Noble)s in early May.\[17\] He then initiated a campaign to consolidate control over key strongholds, marching from [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes) in early June with the ducal banner to capture Champtoceaux, a vital fortress on the Loire River that controlled access to [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) from the south.\[11\] This move aimed to block potential French incursions, as Montfort anticipated opposition from Philip VI, who favored his nephew Charles de Blois. Over the ensuing months, Montfort conducted a rapid tour of the duchy, securing allegiance from several towns and fortresses, including [Rennes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rennes), [Vannes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Vannes), Hennebont, and others, primarily through demonstrations of force and promises of [autonomy](https://grokipedia.com/page/autonomy) to burghers wary of [noble](https://grokipedia.com/page/Noble) dominance.\[15\] These early successes, however, provoked a decisive response from [France](https://grokipedia.com/page/France). In September 1341, the Paris assembly of peers formally awarded the duchy to Charles de Blois, backed by royal armies under commanders like Louis, Count of Spain.\[17\] French-Blois forces advanced into [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany), besieging Champtoceaux, which Montfort had garrisoned but could not hold against the superior numbers. Montfort attempted to relieve the fortress with a [field army](https://grokipedia.com/page/Field_army) from [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes) but suffered defeat in the ensuing clash near Champtoceaux, likely in late October, forcing his retreat.\[18\] Weakened and isolated, Montfort returned to [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes), where local citizens, facing the threat of a prolonged [siege](https://grokipedia.com/page/Siege) and lacking confidence in prolonged resistance, compelled him to negotiate surrender around 1 November.\[11\] Under assurances of [safe conduct](https://grokipedia.com/page/Safe_conduct) for talks, Montfort met with [Blois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blois) representatives but was immediately seized, violating the truce—a tactic enabled by [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) royal authority overriding [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) customs of honorable [parley](https://grokipedia.com/page/Parley).\[17\] He was transported to [Paris](https://grokipedia.com/page/Paris) and confined in the Louvre's towers, remaining imprisoned until March 1345, effectively removing him from the conflict and shifting leadership to his wife, [Joan of Flanders](https://grokipedia.com/page/Joanna_of_Flanders), who rallied Montfort loyalists in [Rennes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rennes) and elsewhere.\[11\] This capture marked the collapse of Montfort's initial territorial gains in eastern and central [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany), though pockets of resistance persisted in the west, setting the stage for English [intervention](https://grokipedia.com/page/Intervention) to counter [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) dominance.\[18\]

### Defense by Joan of Flanders (1341–1342)

Following the capture of her husband, John of Montfort, at [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes) on November 2, 1341, [Joan of Flanders](https://grokipedia.com/page/Joanna_of_Flanders) assumed command of his forces and proclaimed herself Duchess of [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) to preserve their claim against Charles of Blois.\[19\] She rapidly secured key strongholds, including [Brest](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brest) and initially [Rennes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rennes), while dispatching envoys to [England](https://grokipedia.com/page/England) seeking support from Edward III, though immediate aid was limited.\[19\] During the winter of 1341–1342, Joan focused on fortifying Hennebont, her primary base in southern [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany), by reinforcing its walls and stockpiling supplies against anticipated assaults.\[20\] In April 1342, after Charles of Blois captured [Rennes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rennes) in May and advanced southward, he laid [siege](https://grokipedia.com/page/Siege) to Hennebont with a French-backed force, employing twelve siege engines to bombard the defenses.\[21\] \[19\] Joan personally directed the garrison's resistance, arming local women to hurl stones and quicklime at attackers from the ramparts, thereby sustaining morale amid dwindling provisions and intensifying pressure after approximately forty days.\[21\] \[20\] To break the stalemate, she donned armor and led a [sortie](https://grokipedia.com/page/Sortie) of 300 cavalrymen in a nighttime [raid](https://grokipedia.com/page/Raid), setting [fire](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fire) to the besiegers' [camp](https://grokipedia.com/page/Camp) and inflicting significant disruption before withdrawing.\[21\] \[20\] This action earned her the epithet _Jeanne la Flamme_ (Fiery Joan), as chronicled in contemporary accounts emphasizing her audacious leadership.\[21\] Joan briefly evacuated to [Brest](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brest) for reinforcements, returning five days later with about 500 additional troops to bolster Hennebont's defenses.\[21\] \[20\] The arrival of an English fleet under Sir Walter Manny in late spring 1342 provided critical relief, compelling Charles de Blois to lift the siege two days later and retreat, though Joan was compelled to negotiate a temporary truce amid ongoing hostilities.\[21\] \[19\] These efforts preserved Montfort control over western and southern Breton enclaves, preventing total collapse of their position until John's escape in 1343.\[20\] Accounts of her defense, drawn from Jean le Bel's _True Chronicles_ (c. 1360), highlight her tactical acumen in sustaining resistance without direct male leadership, influencing later narratives by Froissart.\[21\] \[19\]

### Escape, English Alliance, and Renewed Fighting (1343–1345)

In early 1343, the Truce of Malestroit, mediated by [Pope Clement VI](https://grokipedia.com/page/Pope_Clement_VI), facilitated John of Montfort's release from captivity in the [Louvre](https://grokipedia.com/page/Louvre), where he had been held since his capture at [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes) in November 1341; the terms required a substantial [surety](https://grokipedia.com/page/Surety) bond to ensure his compliance with [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) oversight.\[22\] Instead of adhering to these conditions and returning to [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) custody, Montfort evaded further detention by departing for [England](https://grokipedia.com/page/England), thereby escaping effective [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) control and preserving his claim to the duchy amid ongoing hostilities.\[23\] This maneuver shifted the conflict's dynamics, as Montfort's flight underscored the fragility of [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) dominance in [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) and opened avenues for external intervention.\[24\] Upon arriving in England, Montfort secured a pivotal alliance with [Edward III](https://grokipedia.com/page/Edward), who formally acknowledged his rights as Duke of Brittany and invested him with the Honour of [Richmond](https://grokipedia.com/page/Richmond)—a traditional English lordship tied to Breton ducal holdings—to solidify the partnership.\[8\] [Edward](https://grokipedia.com/page/Edward)'s support stemmed from strategic imperatives in the [Hundred Years' War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hundred_Years'_War), including countering French influence in [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) and leveraging Montfort's forces to disrupt Philip VI's continental campaigns; in exchange, Montfort pledged [fealty](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fealty) and military cooperation against [France](https://grokipedia.com/page/France).\[25\] This English backing reinvigorated Montfort's position, enabling recruitment of mercenaries and coordination with pro-Montfortist [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) factions, though it also internationalized the succession dispute, intertwining local loyalties with broader Anglo-French rivalries.\[23\] Hostilities resumed in 1345 as Montfort, bolstered by English subsidies and troops, returned to [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) to challenge [Charles](https://grokipedia.com/page/Charles) of [Blois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blois)'s garrisons. He mounted an unsuccessful [siege](https://grokipedia.com/page/Siege) of Quimper, a key Blois stronghold, failing to dislodge defenders despite initial advances, which highlighted persistent divisions among [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) nobles and the logistical strains of divided allegiances.\[26\] Shifting efforts to Hennebont, a Montfortist [bastion](https://grokipedia.com/page/Bastion) previously defended by his wife Joan, Montfort aimed to consolidate control but succumbed to illness—likely [dysentery](https://grokipedia.com/page/Dysentery) or [plague](https://grokipedia.com/page/Plague)—amid the campaign's rigors. He died on 26 September 1345, aged approximately 50, leaving his six-year-old son, [John](https://grokipedia.com/page/John), as heir under English guardianship and prolonging the war's attrition.\[4\]\[23\] Montfort's death marked a tactical setback but sustained the Montfortist cause through English commitment, as Edward III continued patronage of the young claimant against Blois's French-aligned forces.\[8\]

Death, Tomb, and Historical Assessment
--------------------------------------

### Final Siege and Death

In 1345, following his release from French captivity and alliance with [Edward III of England](https://grokipedia.com/page/Edward_III_of_England), John of Montfort returned to [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) at the head of an Anglo-Montfortian army to challenge Charles of Blois's control over key territories. Montfort targeted Quimper, a strategically vital city in Cornouaille held by Blois partisans, launching a [siege](https://grokipedia.com/page/Siege) to reclaim it and bolster his position in western [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany). Despite initial advances, the besiegers faced determined resistance, supply shortages, and counterattacks, leading to the failure of the operation and Montfort's withdrawal.\[4\]\[26\] Retreating to Hennebont, a Montfort loyalist stronghold previously defended by his wife [Joan of Flanders](https://grokipedia.com/page/Joanna_of_Flanders), Montfort succumbed to illness amid the campaign's hardships. He died on 26 September 1345 at the Château d'Hennebont, likely from [dysentery](https://grokipedia.com/page/Dysentery) or a similar camp fever common during prolonged sieges, at approximately age 50.\[4\]\[26\] His death marked the end of his personal involvement in the Breton War of Succession, transferring the claim to his six-year-old son, [John](https://grokipedia.com/page/John) (later John IV), under the regency of Joan, who persisted in guerrilla resistance with English backing.\[8\]

### Tomb and Burial

John of Montfort died of illness on 26 September 1345 at Hennebont, during the unsuccessful siege of Quimper, and his remains were interred in the chapel of the Dominican convent (also known as the [Jacobins](https://grokipedia.com/page/Jacobins)) in Quimperlé.\[27\]\[28\] The burial reflected his disputed status as a [duke](https://grokipedia.com/page/Duke), occurring in a modest, haphazard sepulture rather than a privileged ducal sanctuary, amid the ongoing Montfort-Blois dynastic conflict.\[27\] The original tomb featured a [bronze](https://grokipedia.com/page/Bronze) [effigy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Effigy) or enclosure with a [stone slab](https://grokipedia.com/page/Stone_slab) bearing a simple relief cross, consistent with early 14th-century construction.\[28\] It was later exhumed and reinterred within the same convent's church, though the site fell into neglect and the tomb was profaned during the [French Revolution](https://grokipedia.com/page/French_Revolution).\[28\]\[29\] In 1883, archaeologist Théodore Hersart de La Villemarqué rediscovered remnants of the tomb, including cemented stone walls and bone fragments—[skull](https://grokipedia.com/page/Skull), tibias, [humerus](https://grokipedia.com/page/Humerus), and [ulna](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ulna)—of a man approximately 1.77 meters tall, possibly accompanied by smaller bones of a woman identified as his wife, [Joan of Flanders](https://grokipedia.com/page/Joan_of_Flanders).\[28\] Subsequently, the remains were transferred to the [crypt](https://grokipedia.com/page/Crypt) of the nearby Abbaye Sainte-Croix in Quimperlé, where they were confirmed in 1982.\[30\] No elaborate monument survives, underscoring the clandestine nature of the initial interment and the political marginalization of Montfort's claim by contemporary [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) and [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) authorities.\[27\]

### Evaluation of Achievements and Strategic Impact

John of Montfort's most notable achievement lay in rapidly asserting his claim to the [Duchy of Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Duchy_of_Brittany) following the death of his half-brother John III on April 30, 1341, by seizing [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes) on August 10, 1341, and securing homage from several key Breton towns and nobles who favored male [primogeniture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Primogeniture) over the female-line inheritance designated by John III. This initial success disrupted French-backed efforts to install Charles of Blois, though Montfort's capture at [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes) on November 16, 1341, curtailed further gains. His wife's tenacious defense of remaining strongholds, such as Hennebont, preserved the Montfort position amid French advances.\[31\]\[32\] The decisive strategic pivot occurred after Montfort's escape from French imprisonment in March 1343, when he traveled to [England](https://grokipedia.com/page/England) and pledged homage to Edward III for [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) on March 10, 1343, in exchange for military support. This alliance integrated the Breton conflict into the [Hundred Years' War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hundred_Years'_War), enabling English expeditions such as the 1342 campaign under the [Earl of Northampton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Earl_of_Northampton), which relieved besieged Montfort partisans and established English influence in western [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany). By aligning with Edward's broader claim to the [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) throne, Montfort compelled [France](https://grokipedia.com/page/France) to divert resources, prolonging the war and preventing rapid consolidation under [Blois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blois).\[31\]\[32\] Though Montfort's death from [dysentery](https://grokipedia.com/page/Dysentery) during the siege of Hennebont on September 16, 1345, ended his personal campaigns, his foundational role ensured the claim's endurance through his six-year-old son, later John IV. The English backing he secured facilitated later Montfort victories, including [Auray](https://grokipedia.com/page/Auray) in 1364, which affirmed male-line succession and preserved Brittany's autonomy against [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) overlordship, thereby sustaining it as a contested [frontier](https://grokipedia.com/page/Frontier) in Anglo-French rivalry for decades.\[3\]\[31\]

Battle of Morlaix
=============== 

[British Battles](https://www.britishbattles.com/)

You are here: [Home](https://www.britishbattles.com/) / [100 Years War](https://www.britishbattles.com/one-hundred-years-war/) / Battle of Morlaix

Battle of Morlaix
=================

**_The first land battle between the English and the French of the Hundred Years War fought in Brittany on 30th September 1342_**

[![Image 1: Siege of Hennebont: Battle of Morlaix 30th September 1342 in the Hundred Years War](https://www.britishbattles.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Siege_dHennebont-870x1024.jpg)](https://www.britishbattles.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Siege_dHennebont.jpg)

**Siege of Hennebont: Battle of Morlaix 30th September 1342 in the Hundred Years War**

**The previous battle of the Hundred Years War is [the Battle of Sluys](https://www.britishbattles.com/one-hundred-years-war/battle-of-sluys/)**

**The next battle of the Hundred Years War is [the **Battle of Auberoche**](https://www.britishbattles.com/one-hundred-years-war/battle-of-auberoche/)**

[**To the 100 Years War index**](https://www.britishbattles.com/one-hundred-years-war/)

**Date of the Battle of** **Morlaix**: 30th September 1342

**Place of the Battle of** **Morlaix**: in the North-West of Brittany in France.

**Combatants at the Battle of** **Morlaix**: An English army against a Breton/French army.

[![Image 2: Charles of Blois: Battle of Morlaix 30th September 1342 in the Hundred Years War](https://www.britishbattles.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Charles-of-Blois.jpg)](https://www.britishbattles.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Charles-of-Blois.jpg)

**Charles of Blois: Battle of Morlaix 30th September 1342 in the Hundred Years War**

**Commanders at the Battle of** **Morlaix**: The Earl of Northampton commanded the English army. Charles of Blois, the claimant Duke of Brittany, commanded the Breton/French army.

**Size of the armies at the Battle of** **Morlaix**: The English army comprised around 3,000 men. The army of Charles of Blois is said to have been several times larger than the English.

**Uniforms, arms and equipment at the Battle of** **Morlaix**: The English army comprised a core of knights and men-at-arms with a strong force of archers.

Increasingly during the 14th Century soldiers in an English army in France were all mounted to enable the army to move at speed.

The Battles of Bannockburn in 1314 and Halidon Hill in 1333, both fought against the Scots, moulded English tactics, causing them to abandon the headlong mounted charge and form their armies with knights and men-at-arms as a dismounted central core with the archers pushed forward on the flanks,

The French continued to believe that battles would be won by a massed mounted charge of nobles, knights and men-at-arms delivered against the opposition’s line.

The English had learnt to their considerable cost at Bannockburn the dangers of a mounted attack against a dismounted line armed with spears.

At the battles of Dupplin Moor in 1332 and Halidon Hill in 1333 the English used their archers to strike down the Scots attacks, the stratagem they then pursued so successfully against the French throughout the Hundred Years War.

The weapon of the English archer was a six-foot yew bow discharging a feathered arrow a cloth metre in length. Arrows were fired with a high trajectory, descending on the approaching foe at an angle. The rate of fire was up to one arrow every 5 seconds. For close quarter fighting the archers used hammers or daggers to batter at an adversary’s armour or penetrate between the plates.

the particular strength of the English army lay in its archers with their life-time of training in the use of the longbow, enabling them to deliver a storm of arrows at a high rate of fire.

**Winner of the Battle of** **Morlaix**: The English army repelled at least two French attacks. After the battle both sides initially remained on the battlefield before retreating, the French having suffered significantly more casualties than the English.

**Background to the Battle of Morlaix:**

The 100 Years War between England and France began in 1337. There were a number of issues between the Kings of the two countries. Among them were the security of Gascony for the English King, the encouragement the French Kings gave the Scots to attack England, the English encouragement of rebellion against the French King in the regions of north-eastern France and above all the English Kings’ claim to the throne of France.

During the course of this long war there were periods of French civil war, particularly over the accession to some of the great estates, which the English King exploited by allying himself to one of the sides.

The first of these disputed accessions was over the Dukedom of Brittany.

In April 1341 Duke John of Brittany died leaving no direct heir with his succession in doubt.

The two claimants to the dukedom were Charles, Count of Blois, married to the deceased duke’s niece, Joan of Ponthièvre and John de Montfort, the deceased duke’s step-brother by his father’s second wife, the widow of King Alexander II of Scotland.

Charles of Blois was the nephew of King Philip VI of France, who strongly supported his claim to the Duchy of Brittany.

The claim of John de Montfort was consequently supported by King Edward III of England.

The two parties began a war to take Brittany.

In November 1341, Charles of Blois with a strong Breton/French army captured the city of Nantes and with it John de Montfort, who was imprisoned in Paris.

The resistance on behalf of John de Montfort was continued by his wife, the redoubtable Joan of Flanders.

After some successes, Joan of Flanders was besieged by Charles of Blois in the estuary town of Hennebont in the south-west of Brittainy.

[![Image 3: Joan of Flanders: Battle of Morlaix 30th September 1342 in the Hundred Years War](https://www.britishbattles.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Jan_z_Montfortu-870x1024.jpg)](https://www.britishbattles.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Jan_z_Montfortu.jpg)

**Joan of Flanders: Battle of Morlaix 30th September 1342 in the Hundred Years War**

Joan of Flanders appealed to King Edward III of England for help and a force was dispatched from England under Sir Walter Manny, finally arriving in May 1342 and relieving the now hard-pressed Hennebont garrison, before beginning a campaign against the supporters of Charles of Blois.

On 14th August 1342 another English army landed at Brest on Cape Finisterre, the north-west point of Brittany, comprising 3,000 men commanded by the Earl of Northampton.

Charles of Blois was besieging Brest and was forced by the arrival of Northampton’s army to raise the siege and withdraw to Guingamp, 40 miles to the east.

Northampton advanced to Morlaix and made an unsuccessful attempt to storm the town, before beginning a regular siege.

[![Image 4: Map of the Battle of Morlaix 30th September 1342 in the Hundred Years War: battle map by John Fawkes](https://www.britishbattles.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/MorlaixA-708x1024.jpg)](https://www.britishbattles.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/MorlaixA.jpg)

**Map of the Battle of Morlaix 30th September 1342 in the Hundred Years War: battle map by John Fawkes**

**Battle of** **Morlaix**:

Charles of Blois, invoking his support among the French speaking nobles of northern Brittany, assembled a powerful army, before advancing on 29th September 1342 to relieve Morlaix and give battle to Northampton’s English army.

On hearing of the approach of the French army, the Earl of Northampton left his siege lines outside Morlaix and advanced to meet him.

Northampton’s army took up a position on the road from Morlaix in front of a wood through which the road passed.

The road inclined away from the English position to the east, before rising to the village of Lanmeur, some 2 miles from the wood.

The English army formed a line across the road, its knights and men-at-arms dismounted in the centre with the archers on each flank.

The English dug a trench in front of their line as a trap for the French.

Burne states that the English will particularly have had in mind the effectiveness of the pits dug by the Scots at Bannockburn in 1314.

The trench is said to have been concealed with branches and grass.

As the English can only have been in position a matter of hours before the French attack it must be questioned whether there was time to dig much of a trench.

The French army marched through the village of Lanmeur and began its attack on the English positions at around 3pm.

Charles of Blois’ army was formed in three large bodies of troops, in all several times the size of the English force facing it.

The first body leading the advance west along the Morlaix road was formed of dismounted Breton peasants armed with whatever weapons were available to them.

This body, in reality little more than an armed mob, advanced on the English position.

A single discharge of arrows was sufficient to put the peasant body in swift retreat before it reached the concealed trench.

There was a confused pause, while Charles of Blois contemplated the summary repelling of his first attack, before the second was launched.

The second French attack was made by the knights and mounted men-at-arms, who charged the English line.

This charge was brought up short by the concealed trench, into which the leading ranks fell, under further discharges of English longbow arrows.

A small party of some 200 French horsemen continued the charge beyond the trench but were overcome by the dismounted English men-at-arms, their leader Geoffrey de Charni being taken prisoner.

After a further pause, the third French body of mounted knights and men-at-arms began to advance, spreading out to outflank the now revealed and largely blocked trench and the English line.

His archers short of arrows, Northampton’s army fell back to positions along the edge of the wood. Skirmishing took place, with the French troops spilling around the English flanks.

But the attack on the English positions was not pressed.

Much of the French army had by now left the field, including its Genoese crossbowmen.

As night fell Charles of Blois’ army fell back to Lanmeur, the plan to relieve Morlaix abandoned.

**Casualties at the Battle of** **Morlaix**: French casualties were heavy. 50 knights were killed in the mounted attack on the English line, with 150 taken prisoner, including the commander of the attack, Geoffrey de Charni.

[![Image 5: Image of the beatified Charles of Blois: Battle of Morlaix 30th September 1342 in the Hundred Years War](https://www.britishbattles.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/img-Blessed-Charles-of-Blois-1-1.jpg)](https://www.britishbattles.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/img-Blessed-Charles-of-Blois-1-1.jpg)

Image of the beatified Charles of Blois: Battle of Morlaix 30th September 1342 in the Hundred Years War

Accounts of casualties differ widely, some placing French losses in the tens of thousands. There was no frenzied pursuit so it seems unlikely the French casualties were more than the high hundreds or low thousands, with English casualties perhaps as low as less than a hundred.

Almost certainly the ‘armed peasant’ section of Charles of Blois’ army dispersed to their homes after the battle, making it difficult to assess French losses from the battle as opposed to by desertion.

**Follow-up to the Battle of** **Morlaix**: Charles of Blois was enabled to continue his campaign to take Brittany after a short period of recovery after the battle.

Northampton was unable to take Morlaix and abandoned the siege.

**Anecdotes and traditions from the Battle of** **Morlaix****:**

*   William de Bohun commanded the right flank of King Edward III’s army at the Battle of Halidon Hill against the Scots in 1333, becoming the First Earl of Northampton in 1337.
*   Charles of Blois maintained an ascetic religious life. Following his death in 1364, his cousin the French King Charles V began a move to have Charles of Blois canonized. He was finally beatified in 1904.

13.content:
If you are looking for the page with the statistics about this event you can find it here:[All Statistics](https://phersu-atlas.com/metrics_summary/event/5144.html)

Was a conflict between the Counts of Blois and the Montforts of Brittany for control of the Sovereign Duchy of Brittany, then a fief of the Kingdom of France. The conflict became also a proxy war between England and France.

Chronology
----------

* * *

Interactive Chronologies with maps are available in the section [Changes Navigation](https://phersu-atlas.com/data/event_changes/5144)

*   _April 1365:_ In 1365, under the first Treaty of Guérande, the king of France recognized John IV, the son of John of Montfort, as duke of Brittany.
*   _June 1342:_ Battle of Quimperlé.
*   _January 1345:_ Victorious siege of the city of Quimper by Charles of Blois in 1344.
*   _May 1342:_ Battle of Quimperlé.
*   _August 1352:_ Battle of Mauron.
*   _January 1343:_ Siege of Vannes.
*   _June 1345:_ Battle of Cadoret.
*   _October 1341:_ Battle of Champtoceaux: John of Montfort, the leader of one faction, was made prisoner.
*   _September 1364:_ Battle of Auray.
*   _June 1342:_ The Siege of Hennebont in 1342 was part of the Breton War of Succession. The town was defended by Jeanne de Clisson and her husband Olivier de Clisson against the forces of Charles of Blois, who claimed the Duchy of Brittany. The siege was ultimately unsuccessful, with the town holding out until the arrival of reinforcements.
*   _June 1341:_ John de Montfort settled in Nantes, the capital of the Duchy of Brittany, and seized the ducal treasury at Limoges.
*   _August 1341:_ Jean de Montfort carried out a great ride in his duchy to secure control of the strongholds (Rennes, Malestroit, Vannes, Pontivy, Hennebont, Quimperlé, La Roche-Piriou, Quimper, Brest, Saint-Brieuc, Dinan and Mauron).
*   _May 1342:_ Meanwhile the French took Rennes.
*   _July 1342:_ The Siege of Hennebont in 1342 was part of the Breton War of Succession. The town was defended by Jeanne de Clisson and her husband Olivier de Clisson against the forces of Charles of Blois, who was supported by the French crown. The siege ended with the town successfully holding out and the territory going to Montfort County.
*   _September 1342:_ Battle of Morlaix.
*   _October 1342:_ Battle of Morlaix.
*   _June 1346:_ Battle of Saint-Pol-de-Léon.
*   _July 1346:_ Battle of Saint-Pol-de-Léon.
*   _April 1354:_ Battle of Montmuran.
*   _May 1354:_ Battle of Montmuran.
*   _July 1357:_ Siege of Rennes.

* * *

10.title: Sm9obiBJViBhbmQgdGhlIFN0cnVnZ2xlIGZvciBCcml0dGFueQ==
10.content:
[![Image 1: jan5bretan](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/jan5bretan.jpg?w=122)](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/jan5bretan.jpg)

_John IV de Montfort, Duke of Brittany_

After writing about [Yolande de Dreux](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/2016/10/30/yolande-and-the-hope-for-the-scottish-succession/) a few weeks back, I became intrigued with the story of her grandson, **John de Montfort**.

John was the only son of John, count of Montfort, and [Joan of Flanders](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/2019/08/12/book-corner-joanna-of-flanders-heroine-and-exile-by-julie-sarpy/). He was probably born in November or December of 1339. His great-grandmother was Beatrice of England, a daughter of Henry III, who was the mother of his grandfather, Arthur, duke of Brittany. John is first mention in 1341 when his childless uncle, John III, duke of Brittany, provided him with 20,000 livres from his patrimony. However, when the duke died on 30 April 1341, the duchy was thrown into turmoil. Civil war erupted when John’s father and uncle-by-marriage, Charles de Blois, both laid claim to the duchy.

John de Montfort the elder was the son of Arthur, duke of Brittany, by his 2nd wife, Yolande. Charles de Blois was married to Jeanne de Penthièvre, daughter of Arthur’s second son by his first wife; Guy of Brittany. The bitter conflict was to be absorbed into the much greater struggle, between France and England, that became known as the Hundred Years’ War. Edward III of England supported young John’s father, while Philip VI of France backed Charles de Blois.

In November 1341 John’s father was captured and it was up to his mother to assume the de Montfort cause. Edward III sent troops to secure various strongholds, but by late 1342, after an unproductive campaign, he had minimised his military involvement, leaving a lieutenant in charge as he headed back to England, accompanied by John, who was about 3 years old at the time, his mother and his sister, Joan.

John’s mother was imprisoned in Tickhill Castle, Yorkshire, supposedly after succumbing to a mental illness, though more likely for political reasons. As a result, John was raised in the household of the queen, Philippa of Hainault. Their fortunes revived briefly when John’s father arrived in England 1345, paying homage to Edward III at Easter, having broken his parole and escaped the duchy. He led a small force back to Brittany, but died suddenly in September of the same year, leaving 6-year-old John in the guardianship of Edward III.

[![Image 2: mary_plantagenet_of_brittany](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/mary_plantagenet_of_brittany.jpg?w=189)](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/mary_plantagenet_of_brittany.jpg)

_Mary of England, John’s first wife_

Sir Thomas Dagworth captured Charles de Blois at Le Roche Derrien in June 1347, giving the English the opportunity to discuss the succession issue. It looked for a time, that Edward would sacrifice; in 1353 a treaty was actually drafted that was heavily in de Blois’ favour, depriving John of most of his rights. Luckily, for John, it was never implemented and de Blois was eventually released, in return for a huge ransom, in 1356.

Edward resolved now to back young John’s claims. Around 17-years-old, John experienced his first military campaign when he fought alongside Henry, duke of Lancaster, in the siege of Rennes, from October 1356 to July 1357, and later taking part in the Rheims campaign of 1359-60. In March, 1361, John married Edward III’s daughter, Mary, at Woodstock. The marriage would end in tragedy as Mary, still only 17, died of plague in September of the same year. Discussions throughout the early 1360s offered no lasting political solution and, now having attained his majority, John returned to Brittany in the summer of 1362.

Further discussions hosted by the Black Prince, including plans to partition the duchy, failed. However, when Charles de Blois was eventually defeated killed in battle at Auray on 29th September 1364 Jeanne de Penthièvre was forced to come to terms with John de Montfort and the Treaty of Guérande was signed on 12th April 1365. John was recognised as John IV duke of Brittany  by Charles V of France, to whom he performed homage for his duchy in December 1366.

Initially, as duke of Brittany, John’s ties to England continued to be strong, his financial debts and other obligations ensuring this. In 1366 he married [Joan Holland](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/2015/10/10/the-fascinating-marital-exploits-of-joan-the-fair-maid-of-kent/), step-daughter of Edward, the Black Prince. However, when a lull in the fighting ended in 1369 and France and England were at loggerheads once again, John was caught in a dilemma. As his overlord Charles V was expecting John to fight for France, while Edward III was his old ally and mentor and obviously felt deserving of his loyalty. His prevarications meant his Breton subjects grew restive and when John sided with Edward III, after receiving the earldom of Richmond in 1372 as a sweetener, they openly rebelled.

[![Image 3: joana_canterbury](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/joana_canterbury.jpg)](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/joana_canterbury.jpg)

_Joan of Navarre, John’s 3rd wife_

By April 1373 John had lost everything; he fled to England as his duchy was overrun by French troops. And yet, worse was to follow. After participating in John of Gaunt’s _chevauchée_ from Calais to Bordeaux, John was tried for treason in the Paris _parlement_ in December 1378. In total, John spent 6 years in exile, living on his English estates and attending court and parliament; he was the 1st foreign prince to be made a Knight of the Garter, in 1374.

John was invited to Brittany in 1379 by his Breton subjects, who were beginning to become suspicious of Charles V’s intentions; realising that his attempts to bring Brittany into the French royal demesne would threaten her traditional privileges and independence. The Breton constable of France, Bertrand de Guesclin, deliberately failed to oppose the duke’s landing. After Charles V died in September 1380 a peace was negotiated with the aid of the count of Flanders and Louis, duke of Anjou, which was ratified in the 2nd Treaty of Guérande in April 1381.

A consequence of the treaty was that John de Montfort now opposed his former allies in England and Navarre. With Edward III dying in 1377, his young grandson was now King Richard II. The English still occupied Brest, and John was having difficulties in collecting revenues from his English estates. John’s wife, Duchess Joan, had been staying in England during the troubles but, after much wrangling, was finally returned to her husband in 1382, only to die in November 1384. Her death removed an important connection to the English court and Richard II, her half-brother.

The 1380s saw John consolidating his position in Brittany, making alliances with other French princes, such as the dukes of Berry and Burgundy and the king of Navarre. He developed the duchy’s institutions, encouraged trade, devised new taxes and exploited minting rights. On a cultural level,  John expanded his court and encouraged the arts by extensive patronage. He also encouraged loyalty to his family and dynasty, which was helped greatly by his marriage to Joan of Navarre in 1386 and the birth of his long-awaited heir in 1389.

[![Image 4: 330px-sceau_de_jean_v_-_duc_de_bretagne](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/330px-sceau_de_jean_v_-_duc_de_bretagne.png?w=295)](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/330px-sceau_de_jean_v_-_duc_de_bretagne.png)

_John V, duke of Brittany_

As Anglo-French diplomatic relations thawed in the 1390s, John was able to make a marriage alliance with John of Gaunt, whereby one of his daughters would marry a son of Gaunt’s heir, the earl of Derby. John de Montfort attended the wedding of Richard II and Isabella of France in 1396 and Brest was returned to him in 1397.

Joan and John had an affectionate relationship, producing 8 children, 7 of whom survived to adulthood. John and a second son, Arthur, each became duke of Brittany; Arthur was also constable of France and succeeded his nephew, John’s son Peter, as duke. He died in 1458 and was succeeded by his nephew, Francis, son of his younger brother, Richard, count of Étampes, who had died in 1439. A fourth son, Gilles, died in 1412. Joan and John also had 3 daughters: Marie, countess of Alençon; Blanche, countess of Armagnac and Marguerite, vicomtess de Rohan.

John de Montfort paid one last visit to England in 1398, when he took formal possession of Richmond, attended a Garter ceremony at Windsor and spent some time on progress with Richard II before returning home. He died at Nantes on 1st November 1399, where he was buried. In 1402 his widow, now the wife of Henry IV of England, erected an English-made alabaster tomb over his grave; it was destroyed during the French Revolution. Joan acted as regent for her 10-year-old son, John, until her marriage to Henry; when she entrusted the regency and custody of her Breton children, to the Duke of Burgundy.

Brittany remained an independent duchy within France for another 100 years.

\*

Pictures courtesy of Wikipedia.

\*

Sources: Ian Mortimer _The Perfect King_; Marc Morris _Edward I: A Great and Terrible King_ by Marc Morris;  _Brewer’s British_ _Royalty_ by David Williamson; _The Mammoth Book of British kings & Queens_ by Mike Ashley; _Britain’s Royal Families_ by Alison Weir; _The Oxford Companion to British History_ edited by John Cannon_; The History Today Companion to British History_ Edited by Juliet Gardiner and Neil Wenborn_; The Story of Scotland_ by Nigel Tranter; _Scotland, History of a Nation_ by David Ross; _oxforddnb.com_; britannica.com; W.M. Ormrod _The Reign of Edward III_.

\*

[![Image 5](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/smq-mine.jpg?w=636)](https://historytheinterestingbits.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/smq-mine.jpg)

Scotland’s history is dramatic, violent and bloody. Being England’s northern neighbour has never been easy. Jeanne la Flamme, Duchess of Brittany | Lady Hamilton
=============== 

It's all about the details…

### Search

 

[Lady Hamilton](https://emmaladyhamilton.wordpress.com/)

*   [About](https://emmaladyhamilton.wordpress.com/about/)
*   [Contact](https://emmaladyhamilton.wordpress.com/contact/)

![Image 1](https://emmaladyhamilton.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/03/cropped-elisabeth_vigc3a9e-lebrun_-_lady_hamilton_as_ariadne1.jpg)

[Jeanne la Flamme, Duchess of Brittany](https://emmaladyhamilton.wordpress.com/2012/05/23/jeanne-la-flamme-duchess-of-brittany/ "Jeanne la Flamme, Duchess of Brittany")
========================================================================================================================================================================

[23 May](https://emmaladyhamilton.wordpress.com/2012/05/23/jeanne-la-flamme-duchess-of-brittany/)

Joanna of Flanders was born in 1295, she was the daughter of Louis I, Count of Nevers and Joan, Countess of Rethel, and the sister of Louis I, Count of Flanders.  
She married in 1329 the future John IV, Duke of Brittany, with whom she had two children.

[![Image 2](https://emmaladyhamilton.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/05/countess_jeanne1.jpg?w=490)](https://emmaladyhamilton.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/05/countess_jeanne1.jpg)  
When John’s half-brother (the Duke of Brittany) died in 1341 without male issue, his niece Joanna of Penthièvre and her husband Charles of Blois claimed Brittany. John claimed Brittany for himself, and went to Paris to be heard by King Philip VI of France. Philip was an uncle of Charles, and he imprisoned John, despite having given him a promise of safe conduct.  
Joanna then announced her infant son leader and true heir to Brittany. She mustered an army and captured Redon. From there she went to Hennebont, to prepare it for a siege, and then asked King Edward III of England for aid. This, Edward was eager to give, since he had been claiming the French crown for himself, and he was therefore at odds with Philip. If he could get Brittany as an ally, this would be of great advantage for future campaigns.

[![Image 3](https://emmaladyhamilton.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/05/joanna-of-flanders-history-of-france-guizot-1869-joanna-of-flanders-at-the-relief-of-hennebont-1342.jpg?w=490&h=707)](https://emmaladyhamilton.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/05/joanna-of-flanders-history-of-france-guizot-1869-joanna-of-flanders-at-the-relief-of-hennebont-1342.jpg)  
In the siege of Hennebont by Charles of Blois in 1342, she took up arms and, dressed in armour, conducted the defence of the town, encouraging the people to fight, and urging the women to “cut their skirts and take their safety in their own hands”. When she took a look from a tower and saw that the enemy camp was almost unguarded, she led three hundred men on a charge, burned down his supplies and destroyed his tents. After this she became known as “Jeanne la Flamme”. Charles of Blois tried to starve the people in Hennebont. During a long meeting the bishop of Leon tried to persuade Joanna to surrender, but from the window she saw the ships of Sir Walter Manny’s ships from England sailing up. Hennebont was strengthened with English forces and held out.

[![Image 4](https://emmaladyhamilton.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/05/jeanne-malivels-depiction-of-jeanne-in-her-persona-as-jeanne-la-flamme1.jpg?w=490)](https://emmaladyhamilton.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/05/jeanne-malivels-depiction-of-jeanne-in-her-persona-as-jeanne-la-flamme1.jpg)  
By the treaty of Malestroit in 1343, her husband John was released and hostilities ceased. When her husband died in 1345 in the midst of the Breton War of Succession, she again became the leader of the Montfort party to protect the rights of her son John V against the party led by Charles of Blois and Joanna. In 1347, Joanna’s forces captured Charles of Blois in battle. She was, however, forced to retreat to England. In England, she succumbed to a mental illness, and spent the rest of her life in confinement at Tickhill Castle.  
Joanna was later celebrated for her exploits in Breton folklore, in particular in a ballad collected in Barzaz Breiz.  
She was later known as an earlier patron for women in Brittany, and a possible influence to Joan of Arc of France.
