Date1341 – 12 April 1365[1]
Location

Brittany

ResultTreaty of Guérande
| | Belligerents | | * [House of Montfort-Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Montfort-Brittany "House of Montfort-Brittany") * [Kingdom of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England") | * [House of Châtillon-Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Ch%C3%A2tillon "House of Châtillon") * [Kingdom of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_in_the_Middle_Ages "France in the Middle Ages") * [Kingdom of Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Castile "Kingdom of Castile") | | Commanders and leaders | | * [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort") [#](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_by_natural_causes "Death by natural causes") * [Joan of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort") * [John IV, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany") * [Thomas Dagworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Dagworth "Thomas Dagworth") [**†**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killed_in_action "Killed in action") | [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany "Charles, Duke of Brittany") [**†**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killed_in_action "Killed in action") [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre") | [![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/05/Guerre_de_Succession_de_Bretagne_1341-1364.png/500px-Guerre_de_Succession_de_Bretagne_1341-1364.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Guerre_de_Succession_de_Bretagne_1341-1364.png) Funeral of [John III, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany"), depicted in the Chronicles of [Jean Froissart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Froissart "Jean Froissart") The **War of the Breton Succession** ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _guerre de Succession de Bretagne_; [Breton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_language "Breton language"): _Brezel hêrezh dugelezh Breizh_) or **Breton Civil War** was a conflict between the [Counts of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counts_of_Blois "Counts of Blois") and the [Montforts of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montfort_of_Brittany "Montfort of Brittany") for control of the [Duchy of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Brittany "Duchy of Brittany"), then a [fief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fief "Fief") of the [Kingdom of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France "Kingdom of France"). It was fought between 1341 and 12 April 1365.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession#cite_note-FritzeRobison2002-1) It is also known as the **War of the Two Joans** ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _guerre des deux Jeannes_) due to the involvement of two rival duchesses of that name, [Joan of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort") and [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession#cite_note-2) The war formed an integral part of the early [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") due to the proxy involvement of the French and English monarchs in the conflict; the French supported the Blois (female heir) whilst the English backed the Montforts (male heir). The rival kings supported the duke of the principle opposite to their own claims to the French throne—the [Plantagenet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Plantagenet "House of Plantagenet") having claimed it by female succession, and the [Valois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Valois "House of Valois") by male succession. Montfort was ultimately successful following the [Battle of Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray") in 1364 but, in a surprising turn of events, pledged his loyalty to the king of France and not to the Plantagenet king of England who had supported him. The Breton dukes had both a historical and ancestral connection to Britain and were also [earls of Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earls_of_Richmond "Earls of Richmond") in [Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire "Yorkshire"). Duke [Arthur II of Dreux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_II,_Duke_of_Brittany "Arthur II, Duke of Brittany") married twice, first to Mary of Limoges (1275–1291), then to [Yolande of Dreux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yolande_of_Dreux,_Queen_of_Scotland "Yolande of Dreux, Queen of Scotland") (1263–1322), countess of Montfort and widow of King [Alexander III of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_III_of_Scotland "Alexander III of Scotland"). From his first marriage, he had three sons, including his heir [John III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany") and Guy, [count of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counts_and_dukes_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Counts and dukes of Penthièvre") (d. 1331). From Yolande, Arthur had another son, also named John, who became Count of Montfort. (See [Dukes of Brittany family tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dukes_of_Brittany_family_tree "Dukes of Brittany family tree").) John III strongly disliked the children of his father's second marriage. He spent the first years of his reign attempting to have this marriage annulled and his half-siblings bastardized. When this failed, he tried to ensure that [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort") would never inherit the duchy. Since John III was childless, his heir of choice became [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre"), _la Boiteuse_, daughter of his younger brother Guy. In 1337 she married [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Blois "Charles of Blois"), the second son of a powerful French noble house whose mother's brother was King [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France"). But in 1340, John III reconciled himself with his half-brother, and made a will that appointed John of Montfort the heir of Brittany. On 30 April 1341, John III died. His last words on the succession, uttered on his deathbed, were, "For God's sake leave me alone and do not trouble my spirit with such things". First stage of the war ---------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=War_of_the_Breton_Succession&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: First stage of the war")\] Most of the nobility supported Charles of Blois, so if John of Montfort was to have any chance, it was dependent upon swift action before organized resistance could be made. John quickly took possession of the [ducal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke "Duke") capital [Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantes "Nantes") and then seized the Ducal treasury at [Limoges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limoges "Limoges"). By the middle of August, John of Montfort was in possession of most of the Duchy, the three principal cities of Nantes, [Rennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rennes "Rennes") and [Vannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vannes "Vannes"). Up to this point, the succession crisis had been a purely internal affair. But to complicate things further, the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") between England and France had broken out four years earlier, in 1337. In 1341, there was a truce between the two countries, but there was little doubt that hostilities would be renewed when the truce ended in June 1342. Thus, when rumours reached [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France") that John of Montfort had received English agents, the French Crown naturally took a more direct interest in their small neighbors situation. Charles of Blois became the official French candidate. Whatever had been his original intentions, John of Montfort was now forced to support [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England") as King of France. Edward III was bound by the truce not to take any offensive action in France. Nothing in it, however, hindered France from subduing rebellious vassals. In November, after a short siege and defeat at the [Battle of Champtoceaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Champtoceaux "Battle of Champtoceaux"), John of Montfort was forced to surrender at [Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantes "Nantes") by the citizens. He was offered safe conduct to negotiate a settlement with Charles of Blois, but when this led nowhere he was thrown in prison. It now fell upon John's wife, [Joan of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), to lead the Montfortist cause. Deeming her possessions in the east indefensible, she set up headquarters at [Hennebont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hennebont "Hennebont") in western Brittany but was driven into Brest and besieged, the siege being broken by the arrival of an English army under the [Earl of Northampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_de_Bohun,_1st_Earl_of_Northampton "William de Bohun, 1st Earl of Northampton") at the [naval battle of Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Brest_/(1342/) "Battle of Brest (1342)") on 18 August 1342. Northampton then made his way inland and besieged Morlaix after an unsuccessful initial attack. The siege was lifted after the [battle of Morlaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix "Battle of Morlaix") on 30 September. In Paris it was feared that Edward III would land at [Calais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calais "Calais") once the truce ran out. The major part of the French army was therefore withdrawn, and Charles of Blois was left to pursue his claim on his own. Charles soon proved himself to be an able soldier: Rennes and Vannes were taken and many of the Montfortist captains defected. In late November, [Edward III arrived with his army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III%27s_Breton_campaign,_1342%E2%80%931343 "Edward III's Breton campaign, 1342–1343") at [Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brest,_France "Brest, France"). He almost at once marched against Vannes. [The siege dragged on](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sieges_of_Vannes_/(1342/) "Sieges of Vannes (1342)") and a French army was assembled to meet him, but on 19 January 1343, before any major engagements could be fought, the two kings agreed the [Truce of Malestroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit "Truce of Malestroit"). Vannes was taken into papal custody. With John of Montfort in prison, his son an infant, and his wife recently gone mad, the places under Montfortist control were in practice administered from London, with a large permanent English garrison at Brest. The truce was to last until 29 September 1346 with the hopes that in the meantime the disputes between the two kingdoms could be permanently settled, but in Brittany it made little difference. The truce bound the two kings and their followers, but Charles of Blois claimed to be fighting his own separate war and was therefore not bound by any truce. The brutal small-scale fighting continued at the same pace. In Paris, John of Montfort was released from prison on 1 September 1343 in return for a huge bond and a promise to stay on his estates in the east. The English coastal garrisons held firm, but the Montfortist party continued to crumble. They had some successes, such as the expulsion of the papal custodians from Vannes, but with no unifying leadership, mostly they were reduced to pleading for men and money from London. To hamper communication between Brest and Vannes, Charles of Blois laid siege to [Quimper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quimper,_Finist%C3%A8re "Quimper, Finistère") in early March 1344. The city fell by assault on 1 May and, as usual at that time, this meant the slaughter of civilians in huge numbers, estimated between 1,400 and 2,000. The English prisoners were held for ransom, but the Breton and Norman captives were dispatched to Paris where they were executed for treason. During the summer and autumn, the Montfortist party fell apart. Even those who had been John of Montfort's staunchest allies now considered it futile to continue the struggle. It, therefore, mattered little that in March 1345 John finally managed to escape to England. With no adherents of note of his own, he was now little more than a figurehead for English ambitions in Brittany. Edward III decided to repudiate the truce in summer 1345, a year before it was due to run out. As part of his larger strategy, a force was dispatched to Brittany under the joint leadership of the [Earl of Northampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_de_Bohun,_1st_Earl_of_Northampton "William de Bohun, 1st Earl of Northampton") and John of Montfort. Within a week of their landing in June, the English had their first victory when Sir [Thomas Dagworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Dagworth "Thomas Dagworth"), one of Northampton's lieutenants, raided central Brittany and defeated Charles of Blois at Cadoret near [Josselin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josselin "Josselin"). The follow-up was less impressive. Further operations were delayed until July when Montfort attempted the recapture of Quimper. However, news had reached the French government that Edward's main campaign had been canceled and they were able to send reinforcements from Normandy. With his strengthened army, Charles of Blois broke the siege. Routed, Montfort fled back to Hennebont where he fell ill and died on 16 September. The heir to the Montfortist cause was his five-year-old son, [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"). During the winter, Northampton fought a long and hard campaign with the apparent objective of seizing a harbour on the north side of the peninsula. Edward III had probably planned to land here with his main force during summer 1346. However, the English achieved very little for their efforts. Northern Brittany was Joan of Penthièvre's home region and resistance there was stiff. In the end, Edward decided upon Normandy as the landing spot for his 1346 campaign. Northampton was recalled and Thomas Dagworth was appointed as deputy lieutenant. It was during a tour through the English strongholds on 9 June that Dagworth and his escort were trapped by Charles of Blois and his army near [Saint-Pol-de-Léon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Pol-de-L%C3%A9on "Saint-Pol-de-Léon"). They dug in on a hilltop and fought off all attacks until nightfall when Charles was forced to retreat leaving many of his wounded behind. Tide turns against Charles -------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=War_of_the_Breton_Succession&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Tide turns against Charles")\] [![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/Capture_Charles_de_Blois.jpg/250px-Capture_Charles_de_Blois.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Capture_Charles_de_Blois.jpg) Capture of Charles of Blois At this point events outside Brittany started to have an effect on the war. The French suffered a major defeat at the [Battle of Crécy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cr%C3%A9cy "Battle of Crécy") in 1346, and at Calais in 1347. Without French support, Charles of Blois gradually began to lose ground to the English captains. The memory of the massacre at Quimper increased his unpopularity, and Breton traders had an economic interest in strengthening links with England due to Brittany's strategic position between the Atlantic and English Channel. At the [Battle of La Roche-Derrien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_La_Roche-Derrien "Battle of La Roche-Derrien") in 1347, Charles was taken prisoner as he tried to recapture the town, which had just been taken by the English. He was jailed for five years in the Tower of London. The English now controlled Brest, Quimper, and Vannes. Under pressure from [Pope Innocent VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Innocent_VI "Pope Innocent VI"), the English, French, and Bretons negotiated a peace, while both factions maintained an uneasy balance of power within the duchy. It was during this period that the [Combat of the Thirty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combat_of_the_Thirty "Combat of the Thirty") took place, a famous episode in medieval chivalry. Conflicts between the French and English strongholds of [Josselin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josselin "Josselin") and [Ploërmel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plo%C3%ABrmel "Ploërmel") were resolved in a duel between thirty Montfortist knights led by [Robert Bemborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Bemborough "Robert Bemborough"), and thirty supporters of Charles de Blois led by [Jean de Beaumanoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_de_Beaumanoir "Jean de Beaumanoir"). The combat took place midway between the two towns on 26 March 1351. By nightfall the Anglo-Breton Montfortists had lost nine dead against six of the pro-French knights; the surviving Montfortists were forced to surrender. Though renowned at the time, and later highly romanticised, the combat had no effect on the outcome of the war. [![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/Le_Combat_des_Trente_%281857%29.jpg/250px-Le_Combat_des_Trente_%281857%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Le_Combat_des_Trente_/(1857/).jpg) A 19th-century painting depicting the _[The Combat of the Thirty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Combat_of_the_Thirty "The Combat of the Thirty")_ ([Octave Penguilly L'Haridon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octave_Penguilly_L%27Haridon "Octave Penguilly L'Haridon"), 1857) Edward III signed the Treaty of Westminster on 1 March 1353, accepting Charles of Blois as Duke of Brittany if the latter undertook to pay a ransom of 300,000 crowns, and that Brittany signed a treaty of alliance "in perpetuity" with England; this alliance was to be sealed by the marriage of the Montfortist claimant John of Montfort (son of the earlier John of Montfort) with Edward's daughter Mary. The marriage required the approval of the King of France and a papal dispensation. [Charles de la Cerda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_de_la_Cerda "Charles de la Cerda"), the [Constable of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constable_of_France "Constable of France"), negotiated the deal, but [Charles II of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_Navarre "Charles II of Navarre"), who needed to continue the war between England and France to maintain his own power, decided to intervene by assassinating the Constable. He then switched his support to France in exchange for territory. The treaty was negated, but Charles of Blois had been freed, and returned to Brittany as Duke. [![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Battle_of_Auray_2.jpg/250px-Battle_of_Auray_2.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Battle_of_Auray_2.jpg) The Battle of Auray, 1364 The situation remained in stalemate for some time, with Charles of Blois as _de facto_ Duke, but with significant territory still controlled by the Montfortists. Outside events again began to have an effect on the conflict. A plague struck France and the King himself was captured by the English at the [Battle of Poitiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Poitiers "Battle of Poitiers") in 1356. The French state was virtually paralysed. In 1362, when the younger John de Montfort reached 22 years of age, King Edward permitted him to return to Brittany. His return was conditioned by a covenant not to marry without permission, given in pledge of several fortresses. On arrival, John attempted to reach agreement with Charles of Blois to make peace and share Brittany, but Charles's wife Joan urged him to resist and crush John. The war resumed in 1363 when Charles de Blois, assisted by [Bertrand du Guesclin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrand_du_Guesclin "Bertrand du Guesclin"), had some successes, but when Bertrand left to take control of strongholds in Navarre and Normandy, Charles's advance halted at the unsuccessful siege of Bécherel. Another opportunity to negotiate an agreement arose, but again Joan blocked negotiations. John de Montfort moved to besiege [Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auray "Auray") with renowned English warlord [John Chandos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Chandos "John Chandos"). Charles of Blois and Bertrand du Guesclin came to the rescue of the besieged city, but they were decisively defeated at the [Battle of Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray") on 29 September 1364. This battle marked the end of this long conflict: Charles of Blois was killed and Joan of Penthièvre, finding herself a widow, saw her cause collapse. Du Guesclin was captured and [ransomed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ransom "Ransom") by Charles V for 100,000 [francs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franc "Franc"). Peace was concluded on 12 April 1365 by the [First Treaty of Guérande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Gu%C3%A9rande_/(1365/) "Treaty of Guérande (1365)") which established John of Montfort as Duke of Brittany. He did not reject completely the claims of the Penthièvre family, and established the following law of succession in Brittany: * The Duchy would be transmitted from male to male in the family of Montfort. * In the absence of male offspring, it would switch to males of the family of Penthièvre. * Joan retained the prerogative of Penthièvre and the Viscouncy of Limoges. * She would also receive 10,000 livres of annual rent taken from the French territories of the enemy. King [Charles V of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V_of_France "Charles V of France") did not oppose the elevation of John, fearing that he might declare homage to Edward of England, his protector and former father-in-law (Mary having died in 1361). In addition, France was clearly depleted in the context of the Hundred Years' War. He therefore recognized John as Duke. By this action, he won the friendship of the Breton nobility. In December 1366, he received the oath of the new duke who surprisingly did not pledge allegiance to Edward, recognizing Charles as his sovereign instead. The provisions of the treaty were later repudiated by the Montfortists when a later duke, [John V, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_V,_Duke_of_Brittany "John V, Duke of Brittany") was kidnapped by the Penthièvres in 1420, in violation of the treaty. The Montfortists declared that the treaty had been broken, and as such were no longer required to accept its succession provisions. This became significant when [Francis II, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_II,_Duke_of_Brittany "Francis II, Duke of Brittany") failed to produce a male heir, allowing the duchy to pass to his daughter [Anne of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_of_Brittany "Anne of Brittany") in 1488. * **30 April 1341**: John III dies without heirs. Joan of Penthièvre and Charles of Blois became Duchess and Duke of Brittany. John of Montfort refuses to accept and calls for the help of King [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England"). * **1343**: John of Montfort is taken prisoner, but is released shortly afterwards. Charles tries to take advantage and attacks Hennebont, but the city is defended with success by [Joan of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), wife of Montfort. An English army relieves the siege and forces the Blois to a truce, broken shortly afterwards. * **1344**: Charles takes Quimper with the help of a French army, courtesy of King [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France"), and slaughters 2000 civilians. * **1345**: John of Montfort fails to recover Quimper and dies. His ambitions over Brittany are inherited by his son [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"). His mother, Joan of Flanders, becomes the political and military commander of the Montfort faction. * **Between 1346 and 1364**, several minor battles are won and lost by both parts, several truces are signed and broken. Joan of Flanders becomes mentally ill and is institutionalized in a convent. * **27 March 1351**: [Combat of the Thirty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combat_of_the_Thirty "Combat of the Thirty") * **29 September 1364**: [Battle of Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray"). [Bertrand du Guesclin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrand_du_Guesclin "Bertrand du Guesclin") and Charles of Blois are heavily defeated by John IV and the English warlord [John Chandos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Chandos "John Chandos"). Charles is killed in action, ending the Blois pretensions in Brittany. * **1365**: John IV is recognized as Duke of Brittany and Joan of Penthièvre gives up any claim to the duchy in the [Treaty of Guérande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Gu%C3%A9rande_/(1365/) "Treaty of Guérande (1365)"). Surprisingly, the new duke declares himself as a vassal, not to the English king who helped him, but to King [Charles V of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V_of_France "Charles V of France"). * [List of rulers of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_rulers_of_Brittany "List of rulers of Brittany") * [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") * [List of wars of succession in Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_wars_of_succession_in_Europe "List of wars of succession in Europe") * [War of the Two Pedros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Two_Pedros "War of the Two Pedros") 1. ^ [_**a**_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession#cite_ref-FritzeRobison2002_1-0) [_**b**_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession#cite_ref-FritzeRobison2002_1-1) Ronald H. **John of Montfort** ([Middle Breton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Breton_language "Middle Breton language"): _Yann Moñforzh_, [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _Jean de Montfort_) (1295 – 26 September 1345),[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-1) sometimes known as **John IV**,[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-2) was [Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Brittany "Duke of Brittany") and [Earl of Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Richmond "Earl of Richmond") from 1341 to 1345 in dispute with his niece [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre") and her husband [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Blois "Charles of Blois"). He was also [Count of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_of_Montfort-l%27Amaury "Count of Montfort-l'Amaury") from 1322. He was the son of [Arthur II, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_II,_Duke_of_Brittany "Arthur II, Duke of Brittany"), and his second wife, [Yolande of Dreux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yolande_de_Dreux,_Queen_of_Scotland "Yolande de Dreux, Queen of Scotland"). His contesting of the inheritance of the Duchy of Brittany with his niece Joan led to the [War of the Breton Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession "War of the Breton Succession"), which in turn evolved into being part of the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") between England and France. John's patron in his quest was King [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrevit%C3%A9-Orton1978877-3) He died in 1345, 19 years before the end of the war, and the victory of his son [John IV, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"), over Joan of Penthièvre and Charles of Blois.

[![Image 2: Jean of Montfort's coat of arms.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/Arms_of_Jean_de_Montfort.svg/250px-Arms_of_Jean_de_Montfort.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Arms_of_Jean_de_Montfort.svg "Jean of Montfort's coat of arms.")

Jean of Montfort's coat of arms.

John of Montfort was born in 1295, the only son to Arthur II of Brittany and his second wife Yolande of Dreux.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorge1875table_XXVI-4) In 1322 he inherited from his mother the title of count of Montfort-l'Amaury,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorvan2009table_2-5) and in 1329 he married [Joanna of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort") in [Chartres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chartres "Chartres").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorge1875table_XXVI-4) Joanna was the daughter of [Louis I, Count of Nevers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_I,_Count_of_Nevers "Louis I, Count of Nevers"),[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorge1875table_XXVI-4) and [Joan, Countess of Rethel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan,_Countess_of_Rethel "Joan, Countess of Rethel"). They had:

*   [John IV, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany") (1339–1399), married (1) [Mary of Waltham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_of_Waltham "Mary of Waltham") (1344–1362), daughter of King [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England"), in 1361 in Oxfordshire;[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorge1875table_XXVI-4) (2) [Joan Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Holland,_Duchess_of_Brittany "Joan Holland, Duchess of Brittany") (1350–1384) in 1366 in London;[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorge1875table_XXVI-4) (3) [Joan of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Navarre,_Queen_of_England "Joan of Navarre, Queen of England") (1370–1437), daughter of King [Charles II of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_Navarre "Charles II of Navarre"), in 1386 in Saillé-près-Guérande.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones1988123-6)
*   [Joan of Brittany, Baroness of Drayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Brittany,_Baroness_of_Drayton "Joan of Brittany, Baroness of Drayton") (1341–1402), married before 21 October 1385 to [Ralph Basset, 3rd Baron Basset of Drayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Basset,_3rd_Baron_Basset_of_Drayton "Ralph Basset, 3rd Baron Basset of Drayton")[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChibnall1965130-7)

Succession to Duke John III
---------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_of_Montfort&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Succession to Duke John III")\]

On 30 April 1341, [John III, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany"), died without a male heir. His half-brother, John of Montfort, was a candidate for the succession, which was also claimed by Joan of Penthièvre, niece of John III and wife of Charles of Blois, himself a nephew of the [Philip VI, King of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France"). The King was, of course, favourable to his nephew.

The Duchy of Brittany historically had a "semi-Salic" mode of inheritance; male primogeniture was followed unless no direct male descendants remained. At that point the closest female descendant inherited as duchess, with her husband serving as duke by "right of representation". The position of John of Montfort was legally founded on the belief that a brother (even a half-brother) was a closer heir than a beneficiary niece, and that the Salic form of inheritance adopted by the Kingdom of France should be followed. This argument was based on the fact that since 1297 Brittany had been a _duché-pairie_ ("member and part of the crown"), and that the legislation of the suzerain kingdom should therefore be applied.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeguayMartin198299-8) Challenges to the [Salic law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salic_law "Salic law") of the Franks had historically been rejected for the Kingdom of France, allowing Philip V to gain the throne in 1316, and Philip VI most recently. This made Philip VI's support of Joan of Penthièvre quite ironic, in that the argument for Philip VI to inherit the Kingdom of France was based on the opposing philosophy that the crown should not be able to descend through the female line to Edward III.

A civil war, termed the War of the Breton Succession, then began and lasted 23 years. This conflict was also called _La guerre de deux Jeanne_, after the French names of the two duchesses in competition: Jeanne de Penthièvre and Jeanne de Flanders, wife of John of Montfort.

Early stages of the War (1341)
------------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_of_Montfort&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early stages of the War (1341)")\]

After the funeral of John III, Charles of Blois returned to the Court of France and John of Montfort returned to his Breton estate in [Guérande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gu%C3%A9rande "Guérande"). Then, incited by his wife (according to tradition), he went with a small army to [Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantes "Nantes") where he was well received by the inhabitants who swore their loyalty. John then went to [Limoges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limoges "Limoges") where he managed to obtain the ducal treasury. John returned to Nantes and was recognised as Duke in May 1341 by an assembly composed of members of the towns and minor nobles, but shunned by the major vassals with the exception of Hervé VII, Count of Léon. Thanks to the ducal treasury, he recruited mercenaries which allowed him to perform in June and July a 'great ride in Brittany' (as described by Arthur de la Borderie) and take control of the duchy. John first gained [Rennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rennes "Rennes"), then [Vannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vannes "Vannes") and the places surrounding the [Château de Suscinio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_de_Suscinio "Château de Suscinio"), [Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auray "Auray"), [Hennebont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hennebont "Hennebont"), and then [Quimperlé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quimperl%C3%A9 "Quimperlé"). Having failed to take the domains of [Rohan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Rohan "House of Rohan"), he submitted [Quimper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quimper "Quimper") and [Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brest,_France "Brest, France") before descending to [Carhaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carhaix "Carhaix"), and then went back northward and captured [Saint-Brieuc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Brieuc "Saint-Brieuc"), [Lamballe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamballe "Lamballe"), [Jugon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jugon-les-Lacs_/(delegated_commune/) "Jugon-les-Lacs (delegated commune)"), [Dinan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinan "Dinan"), [Dol-de-Bretagne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dol-de-Bretagne "Dol-de-Bretagne"), and returned to Nantes via [Ploërmel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plo%C3%ABrmel "Ploërmel").

Always accompanied by Hervé VII of Léon, John obtained the submission, if not the support, of some of the major nobles who possessed several of these strongholds and had been loyal to Charles of Blois. However it would probably require getting [Josselin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josselin "Josselin"), or the support of the high secular clergy and great lords, or more, to control the domains of the Penthièvres and the House of Rohan, which represented about two-thirds of Brittany.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEde_la_Borderie1975425%E2%80%93429-9) John also went to England and met with Edward III of England in Windsor, who promised him military assistance and invested him with the [Honour of Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honour_of_Richmond "Honour of Richmond").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeguayMartin1982100-10)

Charles of Blois then made an appeal to Philip VI, who summoned John of Montfort to a Court of Peers session in Conflans in September 1341. In this context by the judgment of Conflans, the Duchy of Brittany was attributed to Charles of Blois. Philip VI agreed to receive _l'hommage lige_ of Charles of Blois on behalf of his wife, and confiscated from John of Montfort the French lands of the County of Montfort-l'Amaury, as well as the Viscounty of Limoges that he held more unduly.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEde_la_Borderie1975430%E2%80%93432-11)

In October 1341, Charles of Blois and [John II, Duke of Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_France "John II of France") (later King of France), put together an army and penetrated into Brittany. They managed to retrieve a number of strongholds which had been lost, including Nantes, which relented on 21 November 1341 after three weeks of siege. John of Montfort was captured and imprisoned in the [Louvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louvre "Louvre") in Paris. Despite the change of camp of Hervé VII de Leon (due to criticisms from John regarding his handling of the siege of Nantes), Joanna, the wife of John of Montfort, continued the armed struggle supported by his allies.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEde_la_Borderie1975441%E2%80%93449-12)

Subsequent stages of the War (1342–1345)
----------------------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_of_Montfort&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Subsequent stages of the War (1342–1345)")\]

After a winter break that ended on 15 April 1342, Charles of Blois resumed the fight and regained a large part of Brittany between May and September 1342. King Edward III of England decided to intervene on behalf of the House of Montfort. Charles de Blois failed to take Hennebont, which was defended by [Joanna of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), while [Robert III of Artois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_III_of_Artois "Robert III of Artois") was mortally wounded besieging Vannes in vain leading an English contingent. In January 1343, through [Pope Clement VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Clement_VI "Pope Clement VI"), a truce was signed at [Malestroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malestroit "Malestroit") to bring peace and the liberation of John of Montfort. The latter was released in September 1343 and retired to England 27 March 1345. His return to the struggle with reinforcements provided by King Edward III of England put an end to the truce. John of Montfort unsuccessfully laid siege to Quimper, then fell ill and died in Hennebont on 26 September 1345.

Tomb of John of Montfort
------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_of_Montfort&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Tomb of John of Montfort")\]

He was buried in the convent of the Dominicans of Quimperlé[\[b\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-13) where his tomb, which had already been desecrated, was found again in December 1883.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEde_la_Villemarqu%C3%A91884278%E2%80%93297-14) His remains are now in the Church of Sainte-Croix de Quimperlé.

Picture](https://www.medievalwomen.org/uploads/5/8/4/5/58454211/published/joanna-of-flanders.png?1497039328)Siege of Hennebont in 1342 CE, Charles de Blois and his forces kept Joanna in the city while they waited for English reinforcements, Chronicles of Jean Froissart © Bibliothèque nationale de France MS 2643 vue 232, folio 104v. ​**Joanna of Flanders ”Jeanne la Flamme”, Jeanne de Montfort**, 1295-1374 _Order of Medieval Women ﻿[Appendix H](https://www.medievalwomen.org/descendants-of-jeanne-la-flamme.html)_﻿ Daughter of Louis I, Count of Nevers and Joan, Countess of Rethel, wife to John of Montfort, the Duke of Brittany.  Joanna fought most of her life in defense of the rights of her husband and later their son’s dukedom of Brittany which was challenged by the House of Blois during the War of the Breton Succession,  an integral part of the Hundred Years War.  Joanna, known for her fiery personality, led the Montfortist cause with considerable skill as a military leader. The rivalry for control of Brittany began with the death of the childless John III, Duke of Brittany.  Two families held rival claims as his successor, the House of Montfort led by John  Montfort and his wife Joanna preferred by the English and the House of Blois led by Charles Blois and his wife Joan of Penthièvre endorsed by the French.  After receiving safe conduct from the king John of Montfort went to Paris to plead his case yet was imprisoned by king Philip VI who, as an uncle to Charles, declared the Blois’ as Brittany’s true heirs. * * *
​Joanna announced their infant son was the leader of the Montfort faction and began to muster an army, leading her army into Redon and capturing the city.  She proceeded to Hennebon but expecting a siege from Charles de Blois sent an emissary, Amaury de Clisson (brother-in-law to Jeanne de Belleville and supporter of the English) to Edward III of England asking for aid.  Edward had already claimed the French crown for himself and realizing it would be wise to have the Duchy of Brittany as a powerful ally against their common enemy the king of France agreed.  During the Siege of Hennebont Joanna took up arms dressed in armor defending the town, urging women to ’cut their skirts and take their safety in their own hands’. When she saw that de Blois had left his rear camp mostly unguarded she quickly gathered 300 of her men to ride out and attack, burning supplies and destroying tents thus earning Joanna the epithet, “Jeanne la Flamme” or “Fiery Joan”.
Jeanne la Flamme, 19th century illustration to Histoire de Notre Breagne, 1922 CE, Jeanne Malivel 1894-1926 CE.
![Image 3: Picture](https://www.medievalwomen.org/uploads/5/8/4/5/58454211/published/joanna-2.png?1499005092)Joanna of Flanders spots English fleet arriving, 1342 CE Illus., François Guizot's, History of France, 1869 CE. Once the Blois army realized what was happening their forces cut Joanna and her troops off from their retreat. The Bishop of Leon tried to persuade Joanna to surrender to Charles de Blois but she refused as she had just seen English ships out in the harbor courtesy of Edward III. Charles de Blois was forced to retreat for the moment although Joanna realized he and his forces would return.  She sailed to England for more reinforcements but was intercepted on the way back by Spanish ships under the command of Louis of Spain, Blois’ ally.  In a hard-fought battle the sailors and knights grappled in hand-to-hand combat as Louis' men attempted to board Joanna's ship. According to Froissart, Joanna fought in person "with the heart of a lion, and in her hand she wielded a sharp glaive, wherewith she fought fiercely".  Eventually the English forces beat off Louis's ships and sailed on to Vannes, a coastal town in north-western France, where Joanna and her troops  took over the city followed by an attack on Rennes which after a long siege was a stalemate resulting in a truce in 1343 and release of Joanna’s husband John IV who died two years later.  When war broke out again the English allied themselves completely with the House of Montfort, capturing Charles de Blois in the name of Joanna who, with her son John V, had taken refuge in England. The war continued until 1364 when the House of Montfort was victorious and their son was named the rightful Duke of Brittany.  Joanna contracted a serious mental illness and was in confinement in England never returning to France, dying in 1374.   It is believed she may have influenced Joan of Arc, another female military leader 50 years later in the Lancastrian phase of the Hundred Year’s War, and was described by  Jean Froissart, French author and court historian,  as having  “the courage of a man and the heart of a lion”.       ​ * * * [Map of Brittany, France](https://www.medievalwomen.org/brittany-france.html) ​**References and Further Reading** * Bell, Jean Le.  _The True Chronicles of Jean le Bel, 1290—1360._  Translated by Nigel Bryant.  Boydell Press,  2011. * “Fiery Joanna”   _Military History Now._  //militaryhistorynow.com/2013/05/15/women-warriors-meet-seven-of-historys-most-amazing-female-commanders/.
