| First phase of the [Breton Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession "War of the Breton Succession") | | --- | | Part of the Breton Civil War and the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") | | [![Image 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/Jan_z_Montfortu.gif/250px-Jan_z_Montfortu.gif)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jan_z_Montfortu.gif)Citizens of [Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantes "Nantes") paying [homage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homage_/(feudal/) "Homage (feudal)") to John and Joanna of Montfort | |
DateMay 1341 – 19 January 1343
Location

Duchy of Brittany

ResultInconclusive (Truce of Malestroit)
| | Belligerents | | * • [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France "Kingdom of France") * • [House of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Blois "House of Blois") | * • [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England") * • [House of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lords,_counts_and_dukes_of_Montfort-l%27Amaury "Lords, counts and dukes of Montfort-l'Amaury") | | Commanders and leaders | | * • [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany "Charles, Duke of Brittany") * • [John, Duke of Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_France "John II of France") | * • [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort") * • [Joanna of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort") * • [William, Earl of Northampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_de_Bohun,_1st_Earl_of_Northampton "William de Bohun, 1st Earl of Northampton") * • [Edward III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England") | The [Breton Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession "War of the Breton Succession") was a dynastic dispute between two claimants to the [Duchy of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Brittany "Duchy of Brittany") which broke out in May 1341, after the death of Duke [John III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany"). A complicating factor was the ongoing [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") between [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France "Kingdom of France") and [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England"). [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France") supported the claim to the duchy of his nephew, [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany "Charles, Duke of Brittany"); [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England") backed the rival claimant, [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort"). John seized most of the fortified places in Brittany in 1341, but a French army sent to support Charles overran eastern Brittany and captured John in November. John's wife, [Joanna of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), took command of her husband's field army, set up her two-year-old son, also named [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"), as the faction's figurehead and heir to his father's claim to the duchy, and appealed for English military intervention. A [truce between France and England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Espl%C3%A9chin "Truce of Espléchin") was in place, but it was due to expire in June 1342. In late May 1342 Charles led an army against the small but strongly walled port of [Hennebont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hennebont "Hennebont") where Joanna was based. Repeated assaults were rebuffed, but the delayed arrival of English reinforcements – caused by lack of shipping and bad weather – forced the Montfortists to retreat to the extreme west of Brittany. The English arrived in August, [relieved Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Brest_/(1342/) "Siege of Brest (1342)") – where Charles was again besieging Joanna – and inflicted a heavy defeat on Charles at the [battle of Morlaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix "Battle of Morlaix"), the first land battle of the Hundred Years' War. Edward III arrived with further English reinforcements, besieged [Vannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vannes "Vannes"), and in turn overran most of Brittany. Attempts to reinforce or supply Edward from England failed and a French army greatly outnumbering the Anglo-Montfortist force was raised and advanced to [Malestroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malestroit "Malestroit"), 18 miles (29 km) from the English camp. Philip entered into negotiations with Edward and the [Truce of Malestroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit "Truce of Malestroit"), which was supposed to pause hostilities for three-and-a-half years, was agreed on 19 January 1343. A peace conference was arranged in [Avignon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avignon "Avignon") where, mediated by [Pope Clement VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Clement_VI "Pope Clement VI"), a treaty to permanently end the war was to be drafted. The conference did not convene until late 1344, due to English quibbling over the arrangements. The proposals made by each side were unacceptable to the other. Neither displayed any willingness to compromise, and the conference rapidly collapsed. After mutual provocations Edward formally renounced the truce on 15 June 1345 and full-scale war resumed. Despite the truce, the Breton Civil War had been grinding on as a disjointed and inconclusive series of petty sieges and skirmishes. The English and their Montfortist allies held almost the whole of Brittany by 1345. The Breton Civil War continued until 1365, the Hundred Years' War until 1453. [![Image 2: a map of France showing only a small part of the south-west under English control](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Francia1328-Shepherd-Simplificado.svg/250px-Francia1328-Shepherd-Simplificado.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Francia1328-Shepherd-Simplificado.svg) France in 1328: English-controlled Gascony is shown in blue in the south west Since the [Norman Conquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Conquest "Norman Conquest") of 1066, English monarchs had held titles and lands within France, the possession of which made them [vassals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vassal "Vassal") of the kings of France. By the first quarter of the fourteenth century, the only sizeable French possession still held by the English in France was [Gascony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gascony "Gascony") in the south west.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption199039%E2%80%9340-1) Following a series of disagreements between [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France") and [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England"), on 24 May 1337 Philip's [Great Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conseil_du_Roi "Conseil du Roi") agreed that the lands held by Edward III in France should be taken back into Philip's hands on the grounds that Edward was in breach of his obligations as a vassal. This marked the start of the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War"), which was to last 116 years.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990184-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger200479-3) On 26 January 1340 Edward formally [claimed the French throne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_claims_to_the_French_throne "English claims to the French throne"). The immediate effect was to allow the [Flemings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flemish_people "Flemish people") to join his cause without technically disowning their fealty to the French crown and therefore becoming rebels. The extent to which Edward considered the claim more than a negotiating position is unclear. In June the French navy was annihilated by the English fleet at the [battle of Sluys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Sluys "Battle of Sluys") and in July Edward [invaded north-east France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tournaisis_campaign_of_1340 "Tournaisis campaign of 1340") at the head of a large, heavily subsidised, allied army. The allies [laid siege to Tournai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Tournai_/(1340/) "Siege of Tournai (1340)") on 1 August. On 7 September the French army arrived, but Philip held it back to ensure there was no risk of a battle occurring. He was probably aware that the allied army was falling apart, with the English unable to pay their allies what they had been promised, or even to feed them. Negotiations for a pause in the fighting were opened, mediated by emissaries of [Pope Benedict XII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Benedict_XII "Pope Benedict XII"). The [Truce of Espléchin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Espl%C3%A9chin "Truce of Espléchin") was rapidly agreed, to last from 25 September 1340 to 24 June 1341. The allied armies left France thereafter.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200235%E2%80%9336-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006299%E2%80%93300-5) The English Crown, bankrupt, was unable to meet its commitments, and Edward fled the continent to avoid his creditors.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers1998233-6) Civil war in Brittany --------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Civil war in Brittany")\] [Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittany "Brittany") was a province of France, but although the [dukes of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dukes_of_Brittany "Dukes of Brittany") were vassals of the [French kings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_kings "French kings") they governed the duchy as independent rulers.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption199017,_34%E2%80%9335-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200662-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones19888%E2%80%9311-9) Nevertheless, when the Hundred Years' War broke out in 1337 between France and [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England") the duke of Brittany, [John III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany") (r. 1312–1341), fought alongside his [feudal lord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudal_lord "Feudal lord") the king of France. John III died on 30 April 1341, leaving a disputed succession, with both his niece, [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre"), and his younger half-brother, [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort"), claiming the duchy. Joan's claim was exercised through her husband, [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Blois "Charles of Blois"), a well-connected and militarily oriented French nobleman who was also a nephew of King Philip of France.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990370%E2%80%93371-10)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199966%E2%80%9367-11)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGraham-Goering202047%E2%80%9349-12) On John III's death John of Montfort acted quickly and installed friendly garrisons in most of the towns and castles of Brittany by August.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990377%E2%80%93378-13) The [Parlement of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parlement_of_Paris "Parlement of Paris") was the supreme judicial authority in France[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990377%E2%80%93378-13) and on 7 September, at Philip's urging, it declared that Charles of Blois was the legitimate successor to John III.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007203-14) Philip found the idea of having a relative as the duke attractive because it would bring the traditionally semi-autonomous province more firmly under royal control. He was willing to commit considerable military resources to achieve this and despatched an army, commanded by his eldest son, [John, Duke of Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_France "John II of France"), to support Charles.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllmand200114-15) This army overran all of eastern Brittany except [Rennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rennes "Rennes") and took John of Montfort prisoner.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990389-16)[\[note 1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-19) John's wife, [Joanna of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), was in Rennes when news of John's capture arrived. She acted decisively, recalled the field army from western Brittany, took command[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990389%E2%80%93390-20)[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007204-21) and moved to [Hennebont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hennebont "Hennebont"), a small but strongly walled town with access to the sea. From there Joanna retained control of most of western Brittany[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990389%E2%80%93390-20) and set up her two-year-old son, also named [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"), as the faction's figurehead and heir to his father's claim to the duchy.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVisserSnijder201433%E2%80%9334-22) She despatched her senior counsellor, [Amaury of Clisson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amaury_of_Clisson "Amaury of Clisson"), to [Edward III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III "Edward III"), the English king, with the ducal treasury to encourage English military intervention and waited on events.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990389%E2%80%93390-20)[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007204-21) On 21 February 1342 Edward sealed a treaty to support the Montfort cause as an extension of the war with France.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod199017-23)[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990390-24) Edward saw the opportunity to set up a ruler in Brittany at least partly under his control; this could provide access to Breton ports which would greatly aid England's naval war and give ready entry to France for English armies.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllmand200114-15)[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway2011109-25) In May 1342 [Clement VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clement_VI "Clement VI") became pope. He was strongly pro-French and had previously been one of Philip's senior advisers. He despatched two cardinals to attempt to broker a permanent settlement of the Anglo-French war. The following month they were well received by Philip in Paris; Edward, on the other hand, would not even allow them to cross [the Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Channel "The Channel").[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990395%E2%80%93396-26) English intervention -------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: English intervention")\] [![Image 3: Colour photograph of a small medieval-era single-masted sailing ship](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/Ubena_von_Bremen_Kiel2007_1_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Ubena_von_Bremen_Kiel2007_1_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ubena_von_Bremen_Kiel2007_1_/(cropped/).jpg) In 1962 a well-preserved wreck of a cog dated to 1380 was found near Bremen, Germany. This is a full-size reproduction. Merchant vessels such as these formed the bulk of the English fleet.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger2004120-27)[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTERose200716-28) A map of Brittany, with modern administrative boundaries, showing the locations of some of the places mentioned in the text English reinforcements took a long time to arrive and in May 1342 Rennes fell, allowing Charles to march on Hennebont, part of a general offensive to push his area of control westward.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990391,_393-29)[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007204-21)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway2011109%E2%80%93111-30) On arrival at Hennebont several units of Charles's army advanced against orders and attacked some of the town's defenders who were formed up outside its gate. More troops were pulled into this fight before the French were pushed back in a disorderly retreat. The Montfortists pursued, inflicting many casualties and burning the French camp. According to a contemporary account Joanna rode through the suburbs in full armour encouraging the fighting men.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007204-21) Two days later the French launched a series of better-planned assaults on the town's walls, but all were repulsed with losses.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVisserSnijder201436-31) The main French force moved on, leaving a detachment to carry out a regular siege in an attempt to starve the town into surrender.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990394%E2%80%93395-32) A fleet of French and mercenary [galleys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galley "Galley") cruised off the north Breton coast, but there was so little English naval activity that they were beached and their crews went ashore to fight as infantry. Edward planned to land in Brittany himself in June with a substantial force, but extreme difficulty in assembling ships,[\[note 2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-35) despite draconian measures taken by Admiral [Robert Morley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Morley,_2nd_Baron_Morley "Robert Morley, 2nd Baron Morley"), and then contrary winds, caused this date to be repeatedly put back.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990391,_393-29)[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007204-21)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway2011109%E2%80%93111-30) While waiting for English reinforcements the flow of events went against the Montfortists in the face of Charles's huge military superiority. Having taken Vannes,[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998139-36) he moved on to besiege Auray and, again, Hennebont; both fell. By August little was left to Jeanne's forces, most of whom were besieged in the western port of [Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brest,_France "Brest, France") by a large army and blockaded from the sea by 14 mercenary [Genoese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genoa "Genoa") galleys.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990393,_397%E2%80%93398-37) Brest was on the brink of surrender when the English arrived on 18 August. Their fleet of 140 converted merchantmen and an unknown number of galleys took the Genoese galleys by surprise and 11 were burnt.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger2004100-38)[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998139-36) The English ships carried 1,350 men,[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger2004100-38) a force far inferior to that of the French besieging Brest. But, seeing so many English ships crowded into the [Brest Roads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roadstead_of_Brest "Roadstead of Brest") and the English [vanguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanguard "Vanguard") disembarking onto the beach, they anticipated an attack by a vast host. Charles promptly broke off the siege and withdrew 65 kilometres (40 mi), abandoning western Brittany, where the populace strongly favoured the Montfort cause.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199970-39)[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990399%E2%80%93400-40) Part of Charles' force withdrew along the south coast of Brittany, but the bulk of the army accompanied him to [Guingamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guingamp "Guingamp").[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990400-41) Here he concentrated his forces and called up local levies.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199970-39) The English were commanded by [William, Earl of Northampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_de_Bohun,_1st_Earl_of_Northampton "William de Bohun, 1st Earl of Northampton"), who was reinforced by 800 men under [Robert of Artois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_III_of_Artois "Robert III of Artois") a few days after landing. He also absorbed several other small English forces and an unknown number of John of Montfort's Breton partisans.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990400-41) Northampton's first mission was to secure a port for the main English army to disembark at.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990400-41) [![Image 4: A pen and ink drawing of the head and shoulders of a bearded man in early modern style](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/CarlosIdebritania.jpg/240px-CarlosIdebritania.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CarlosIdebritania.jpg) Charles of Blois as envisaged in 1621[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBritannica2018-42) The English marched 30 miles (50 km) from Brest to Morlaix, a port on the north coast of Brittany with strong fortifications and a secure harbour, and laid siege to it.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199970-39)[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990399%E2%80%93401-43) Edward's contingent was still in England waiting for the ships which had transported Northampton's echelon to return. The French mistakenly believed this army would be used in north-east France, probably disembarking in [Picardy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picardy "Picardy"). A French army was gathered to confront this imagined threat, including many men transferred from Brittany. Charles became aware his force greatly outnumbered the English, despite the detachments to Picardy, and took his army west in an attempt to relieve Morlaix. [\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990401%E2%80%93402-44) Warned of this, the English carried out a night march and prepared a defensive position on the Guingamp-Morlaix road.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199971%E2%80%9372-45) When they sighted the English position, the French deployed into three divisions, one behind the other.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennett19995-46)[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199972%E2%80%9373-47) The first of these, probably made up of Breton [levies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudal_levies "Feudal levies"), advanced and was shot to pieces by the English archers using [longbows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longbow "Longbow"); it then broke without making contact.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199973-48)[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006222-49) The second division, of French and Breton [men-at-arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Men-at-arms "Men-at-arms"), attacked but their charge was halted when they fell into a camouflaged ditch in front of the English position. Presented with a large, close-range target the English archers inflicted many casualties.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006222-49)[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990402-50) About 200 French cavalry made their way over the ditch and came to grips with the English men-at-arms, who were fighting on foot. This band was cut off by the English and all were killed or captured.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199973-48) Northampton was concerned that the English archers were running out of arrows and that the ditch was so full of dead and wounded men and horses as to be ineffective as an obstacle. Therefore, when the third French division was seen to be preparing to attack the English withdrew into a wood to their rear.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199973-48)[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006222%E2%80%93223-51) The French were unable to force their way in, so they surrounded it and besieged the English, possibly for several days. Northampton broke out with a night attack and returned to Morlaix.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennett19996-52)[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990402-50)[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199975-53) Charles gave up his attempt to relieve the town and retreated.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199975-53) This was the first major land battle of the Hundred Years' War[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200237-54)[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006222-49)[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990483-55) and the tactics used foreshadowed those of both the French and the English for the rest of the 1340s.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennett19996-52)[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199975%E2%80%9376,_112%E2%80%93113-56) On 6 October Edward abandoned his [siege train](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Train_/(military/) "Train (military)") on the beach and set sail from England with those troops he was able to embark onto the available shipping. They reached Brittany after a storm-wracked three-week passage.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway2011112%E2%80%93113-57)[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990401,_403-58) After concentrating at Brest, the English and Montfortist force moved on the major city of [Vannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vannes "Vannes"), the second most populous settlement in Brittany, with a good harbour and walls. From Vannes a strong detachment could control much of southern Brittany. On 7 November both the navy and the army set off. The fleet was depleted by the desertion of most of its ships; their masters and crews were unhappy at not being paid and at being forced out to sea in dangerous winter weather.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway2011113-59)[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990403%E2%80%93404-60)[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFr%C3%A9laut200535-61) Those left sailed to Vannes, enduring a winter storm en route. They attempted to take the town with a surprise attack; this came close to success but was defeated.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990404%E2%80%93405-62)[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway2011113-59)[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger2004102-63) In England the [King's Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curia_regis "Curia regis") attempted to organise a further fleet to carry supplies and reinforcements. Fifty-six ships sailed on or after 3 November carrying 600 men, but were driven ashore in the [Isles of Scilly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isles_of_Scilly "Isles of Scilly") by further storms. They and 800 men who had not sailed waited for a break in the weather, fruitlessly: they were finally [stood down](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/stand_down "wikt:stand down") in February 1343.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990406-64)[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway2011113-59) The main Anglo-Breton army marched unopposed 120 miles (190 km) through southern Brittany and on 29 November attempted to take Vannes by storm. The French garrison had been newly reinforced and repelled this assault; a regular siege began.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990405%E2%80%93406-65) The siege did not require the entire army and large detachments were sent on [chevauchees](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/chevauchee "wikt:chevauchee") across eastern Brittany to devastate the region and capture the fortified places. The outskirts of [Dinan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinan "Dinan") and the area around [Dol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dol-de-Bretagne "Dol-de-Bretagne") were devastated, 100 miles (160 km) north of Vannes.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990405%E2%80%93406-65) [Ploërmel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plo%C3%ABrmel "Ploërmel"), [Malestroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malestroit "Malestroit") and [Redon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redon,_Ille-et-Vilaine "Redon, Ille-et-Vilaine") were captured and [Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantes "Nantes"), the ducal capital, was besieged.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200660,_207-66) Increasing numbers of Breton knights and lords switched their allegiance to the Montfortist cause. However, there were fewer than 5,000 English troops in Brittany, and the term of service of many was running out.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990406-64) No food supplies were arriving for Edward by sea, and although he sent out foraging columns over a broad area, living off the land in winter yielded thin returns. Edward's army was in difficulty.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007206-67)[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger2004102-63) [![Image 5: See caption](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Malestroit_-_Chapelle_de_la_Madeleine_plaque.JPG/250px-Malestroit_-_Chapelle_de_la_Madeleine_plaque.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Malestroit_-_Chapelle_de_la_Madeleine_plaque.JPG) The commemorative plaque on the ruins of the [Chapel of the Madeleine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_the_Madeleine,_Malestroit "Chapel of the Madeleine, Malestroit") where the truce was sealed,[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006207-68) reads: "Historic ruins of the Magdalene chapel, where was signed on 19th January 1343 during the Hundred Years' war by representatives of the English and French realms, the Truce of Malestroit, in the presence of Papal legates the Cardinals of Clermont and Prenets."[\[note 3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-70) The French were perturbed by Edward's landing in Brittany, when he was expected to invade further east, and by his taking the field so late in the season, when their armies had been disbanded. During November they struggled to put together an army and to accumulate sufficient supplies to feed and equip it. The army was based at the major French supply centre of [Angers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angers "Angers")[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990386,_406%E2%80%93407-71) with John, Duke of Normandy, again in command.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006207-68) There are no contemporary figures on the size of the French army, but it was several times larger than the Anglo-Breton force.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007207-72) It was 14 December before the French began the 50-mile (80 km) journey west to the Breton border. Edward was sufficiently alarmed to invite the two cardinals he had brushed off in the summer to present their credentials. They had been observing events from [Avranches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avranches "Avranches"), just over the Breton border, and were allowed no closer than Malestroit, 18 miles (29 km) from the main English camp. Edward suspected that details of everything they saw would be passed on to the French and took great care not to betray the small size and poor state of his army.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990406%E2%80%93407-73)[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006207-68) Once started, the French advance was rapid; it was Christmas Day (25 December) 1342[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199984-74) when the French relieved Nantes. Redon, Ploërmel and Malestroit were recaptured during early January and the French encamped around the latter. The two cardinals were probably in Malestroit when it fell to the French, on or shortly after 10 January.[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990386,_406%E2%80%93407-71) As in 1340 the French were content to threaten the English, without moving close enough for serious fighting to be a possibility. With both sides disinclined to commit to battle, negotiations were entered into.[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich1980174-75) Philip VI set up his court at Redon from where he sent emissaries to the cardinals. By 19 January 1343 the terms of a truce had been agreed and it was sealed; the break in hostilities was to last until 29 September 1346.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990407%E2%80%93408-76) The historian [Jonathan Sumption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Sumption,_Lord_Sumption "Jonathan Sumption, Lord Sumption") describes the terms as "astonishingly favourable" to the English.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990407%E2%80%93408-76) Both France and England were to retain the territory they held when the truce came into effect: this applied to Brittany, Gascony, [Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flanders "Flanders") and [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland "Scotland").[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990409-77) Vannes was to be held by the papacy for the duration of the truce, Philip was to immediately free John of Montfort[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006207-68)[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007207-72) and there was a general exchange of prisoners.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones1988208,_n._30-78)[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEB%C3%A1r%C3%A1ny1997225-79) Both monarchs pledged to negotiate a treaty to permanently end the war, in [Avignon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avignon "Avignon"), then the [seat of the Papacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avignon_Papacy "Avignon Papacy"); with the process to be mediated by Clement. In reality each saw the truce as a mere pause and neither intended to negotiate in good faith; the truce had only been agreed because each king felt it was beneficial to him.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990408-80)[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006110-81) [![Image 6: a water colour image of the head and shoulders of a man wearing a white papal hat](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/01_Cl%C3%A9ment_VI_%28Fresque_de_la_chapelle_Saint-Martial_du_palais_des_papes%29.jpg/250px-01_Cl%C3%A9ment_VI_%28Fresque_de_la_chapelle_Saint-Martial_du_palais_des_papes%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:01_Cl%C3%A9ment_VI_/(Fresque_de_la_chapelle_Saint-Martial_du_palais_des_papes/).jpg) Pope Clement VI, pictured on the wall of the Chapel of Saint-Martial in the [Papal Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais_des_Papes "Palais des Papes") in Avignon. Clement commissioned the decoration of the chapel, which was completed during his lifetime.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTELuyster2011334-82) Edward left for England, enduring another winter storm which scattered the fleet, sinking several ships, He arrived on 1 March.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007209-83) Philip believed that with the fighting ended, all the English would leave for home, as they had left north-east France after the Truce of Espléchin. He was mistaken, and the Breton Civil War ground on in a series of petty skirmishes, despite the truce.[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich1980174-75)[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200245-84) The English and their Montfortist allies held almost the whole of Brittany by 1345.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoskins201113-85)[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESadler2013211-86) John of Montfort was not released until September, despite the treaty's stipulations.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990409,_432-87) Late in 1343 the citizens of Vannes rose against the Pope's authority, expelled his garrison and delivered the town to the English, who held it until the end of the Breton Civil War in 1364.[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990432-88)[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFr%C3%A9laut200535-61) The English did not trust Clement and repeatedly delayed sending delegates to the envisaged peace talks. When the conference finally convened in late 1344 the proposals made by each side were unacceptable to the other, with neither displaying any willingness to compromise, and it rapidly collapsed.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200639-89) Neither monarch took the provisions of the truce agreement seriously; the fighting had continued much as before in Brittany and Gascony. Edward was planning another major invasion of France long before the truce was due to expire in September 1346.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEB%C3%A1r%C3%A1ny1997225-79) During the summer of 1343 [Olivier of Clisson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olivier_IV_de_Clisson "Olivier IV de Clisson"), a senior Breton lord, was invited from England to a tournament on French soil. As he was protected by the treaty he attended, but on the orders of the French king was arrested for treason and executed without trial.[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBoveBiget2013131-90)[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBordonove200674-91) Edward formally renounced the truce on 15 June 1345, at which Gascony [reverted to full-scale war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gascon_campaign_of_1345 "Gascon campaign of 1345").[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEB%C3%A1r%C3%A1ny1997225-79) Edward personally led another expedition to France in 1346, this time [landing in Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cr%C3%A9cy_campaign "Crécy campaign").[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006xxxvi%E2%80%93xxxvii,_39-92) His army was wholly English and Welsh and it laid waste to a 40-mile-wide (64 km) strip of some of the richest lands in France to within 2 miles (3 km) of Paris, [sacking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Looting "Looting") many towns on the way. On 26 August 1346 Philip was finally provoked into attacking at the [battle of Crécy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cr%C3%A9cy "Battle of Crécy"), where the French were defeated with a heavy loss of life.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200239%E2%80%9340-93)[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006105%E2%80%93106-94)[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers2014252,_257-95) In the aftermath of this battle the English [laid siege to the port of Calais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Calais_/(1346%E2%80%931347/) "Siege of Calais (1346–1347)"), which fell in August 1347. The [Truce of Calais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Calais "Truce of Calais") was subsequently sealed on 28 September; originally due to expire on 7 July 1348, it was repeatedly extended until 1355, when full-scale war broke out once again.[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200673%E2%80%9375-96) Joanna of Montfort travelled to England in 1343 and took no further part in the war, dying in September 1374. She stayed in Tickhill Castle and it was given out at the time that she had gone insane; this is accepted by most historians although it has been suggested that she was confined for political reasons, rather than because of mental illness.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990409-77)[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESarpy2019section_%22political_prisoner%22-97) John of Montfort died in 1345,[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998139-36) but the Breton Civil War continued as a disjointed and inconclusive sequence of sieges, skirmishes and truces, frequently as part of the Hundred Years' War. The eastern and southern parts of Brittany were mostly held by the French, who continued to strongly support Charles of Blois, while western and northern Brittany continued to be largely Montfort or English controlled.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200237-54) Charles of Blois was killed in 1364 at the [Battle of Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray") and his army decisively defeated. The next year his widow, Joan of Penthièvre, signed the [Treaty of Guérande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Gu%C3%A9rande_/(1365/) "Treaty of Guérande (1365)"), recognising John of Montfort's son as Duke of Brittany, which ended the war.[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich1980174-75)[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200245-84)[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones1999106-98)[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200692%E2%80%9393-99) The Hundred Years' War continued until 1453, when it ended in a French victory.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006l-100) Notes, citations and sources ---------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343&action=edit§ion=7 "Edit section: Notes, citations and sources")\] 1. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_ref-19)** John surrendered on the granting of a [safe conduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safe_conduct "Safe conduct") to Paris and back by [John, Duke of Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_France "John II of France"), King Philip's oldest son, who escorted him. [![Image 1](https://i0.wp.com/thefreelancehistorywriter.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/202112-2_countess-jeanne-de-montfort.jpg?resize=338%2C450&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/thefreelancehistorywriter.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/202112-2_countess-jeanne-de-montfort.jpg?ssl=1)

**Jeanne “la Flamme”, Duchess of Brittany ~ A guest post by Simon Duits**

The Freelance History Writer is pleased to welcome historian Simon Duits as a guest on the blog with an article on French/Breton history. He writes extensively about the Middle Ages over at [MedievalReporter.com](https://medievalreporter.com/).

During the chaos and confusion of the early Hundred Years’ War, a woman of fiery character led the Duchy of Brittany into battle. Strong-willed and courageous, her ferocious personality earned her the epithet “la Flamme” or, “the Flame”. Her name was Jeanne. She eventually even had the rare honor of having a war named after her, as the War of the Breton Succession also became known as the “War of the Two Jeannes” – one of them, of course, being Jeanne la Flamme. She spent much of her life pouring her energy into this cruel contest.

At the time, succession struggles were all the rage across late medieval Europe. Only four years before the Breton War erupted, the Hundred Years’ War had kicked off. [Claimants from the Houses of Plantagenet and Valois](https://thefreelancehistorywriter.com/2016/04/15/salic-law-and-the-exclusion-of-women-from-the-crown-of-france/) went to war over the right to rule France. The late French king, Charles IV “the Fair”, had died without issue in 1328. Both his cousin – King Edward III of England (Plantagenet) – as well as his nephew – Count Philip (Valois) – claimed the French throne.

In 1341, the War of the Breton Succession erupted against this backdrop. The same thing that had happened to the French crown happened to the Duchy of Brittany: its ruler died without direct male descendants. Again, two factions went to war over the spoils of succession. Because the Hundred Years’ War was already raging across France, the Breton succession struggle soon became a proxy conflict of the larger theater of war between the English and the French. Both London and Paris intervened heavily in Brittany’s affairs during this period – and thus in Jeanne la Flamme’s life.

**The War of the Breton Succession**

Jeanne was born as Joanna of Flanders, daughter of the count of Nevers in western Burgundy and the countess of Rethel in northern Champagne. She carried the Flemish name on account of her brother, who became Count of Flanders in 1328 and steered the county into a pro-French course. Later, he was duly killed in the famous Battle of Crécy by the English.

In 1329, Jeanne married John of Montfort, the half-brother of the Breton duke. When this duke died childless, a contentious succession dispute dragged the entirety of Brittany into open war. The reason for this was that, for a long time, the late duke had declared his niece Jeanne de Penthièvre as heir. She was married to Charles of Blois, who would thus become the next Duke of Brittany. But, just before passing away, the dying duke indicated that his half-brother John of Montfort – Joanna of Flanders’ husband – should be his successor.

Upon the duke’s death in April, 1341, John and Jeanne predictably pressed their claim. Charles of Blois and Jeanne de Penthièvre naturally did the same. The stage for the War of the Two Jeannes was set.

John of Montfort and Jeanne of Flanders moved as quickly as they could. They secured the ducal treasury, hired some mercenaries, and – with this makeshift army – managed to subdue several castles and cities. Rennes, Vannes, Hennebont, Brest, Dol-de-Bretagne, and other strategic sites declared for the Montfortist cause. On top of that, an assembly of the citizens and lower nobility of the important city of Nantes acknowledged John as Duke of Brittany. John and Jeanne enjoyed a clear first mover advantage.

[![Image 2](https://i0.wp.com/thefreelancehistorywriter.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/202112-2_jeanne-and-john-at-court.jpg?resize=809%2C942&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/thefreelancehistorywriter.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/202112-2_jeanne-and-john-at-court.jpg?ssl=1)

Jeanne and John are declared Duchess and Duke of Brittany by the inhabitants of Nantes. (15th century, Public Domain)\]

However, the high nobility, who controlled roughly two-thirds of the duchy, had not chosen sides yet. One of the major Breton houses were the Penthièvres – the House of the “other Jeanne”, wife of the opposing claimant Charles of Blois. To make matters even more complicated, Charles of Blois was a cousin of Philip of Valois – the new King of France and the very reason for the commencement of the Hundred Years’ War. In response, John of Montfort made a fateful decision that plunged the Breton dispute into the larger Anglo-French conflict, and sought the assistance of the king of England to balance things out.

**The English Connection**

John met with Edward III at Windsor. The English king pledged to support the Montfortist cause with troops and money in return for Brittany recognizing Edward as its lawful suzerain. This was precisely what the French feared. King Philip VI was not prepared to engage in a protracted proxy war over the Breton peninsula. The Hundred Years’ War already had enough fronts as is. Therefore, the French king summoned both John of Montfort and Charles of Blois to Paris. Philip VI wanted to settle this dispute without spilling any more blood.

The two claimants met during the Court of Peers meeting that King Philip VI had assembled. Quite unsurprisingly, neither side was willing to concede their point. So, the French king took a simple yet significant decision: he imprisoned John on the grounds of conspiring with the English and attributed the Duchy of Brittany to his cousin, Charles of Blois. One could be forgiven for thinking that this was an effective “quick and dirty” solution to one of the many challenges facing the French king at the time. Before the first English soldier had set foot on Breton soil, the succession war seemed already concluded.

But, in a spectacular turn of events, John of Montfort escaped his Paris prison, fled to Brittany and gathered his army. The French dreaded the idea of the English landing in Brittany, so Philip VI responded posthaste. He dispatched Charles of Blois to Brittany to settle the issue militarily once and for all. A French army over 7,000 strong appeared in front of the city walls of Nantes before the year 1341 was out.

The French made it very clear what they would do to treasonous Bretons if they didn’t surrender. They executed Montfortists taken prisoner in sight of the walls and catapulted the decapitated heads inside the city. The assembly that had declared for John only months earlier was enraged at the course of recent events and forced John to surrender. He gave in and was – once again – imprisoned in the Louvre in Paris.

Thanks to friends in high places, Charles of Blois had won the day. His uncle, the King of France, had personally made him Duke of Brittany. John’s brief stint as duke and his rapid downfall caused Montfortist morale to drop to an all-time low. Many members were considering the cause lost and regarded it futile to defy the French any longer. But Jeanne of Flanders, who had not been present at the siege of Nantes, was quite unwilling to surrender.

With her husband in prison once again, it fell upon her to lead the Montfortist cause. As one contemporary chronicler put it, “\[with\] the courage of a man and the heart of a lion”, Jeanne lifted her soldiers’ spirits and reassured them of the rightfulness of her husband’s claim. Bellicose as ever, under her leadership, the House of Montfort geared up for another round of fighting.

**A Flame Erupts**

With winter approaching (Charles of Blois conquered Nantes in November, 1341), hostilities ceased for the moment. This gave Jeanne of Flanders ample time to prepare for the next year of campaigning. She based much of her hope on the English reinforcements still making their way to Brittany. Consequently, she decided she would buy as much time as possible. Looking for a place to stall the advance of Charles of Blois into Brittany proper, she picked the castle of Hennebont on the southern Breton coast.

[![Image 3](https://i0.wp.com/thefreelancehistorywriter.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/202112-2_jeanne-at-hennebont_1.jpg?resize=564%2C814&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/thefreelancehistorywriter.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/202112-2_jeanne-at-hennebont_1.jpg?ssl=1)

Jeanne at Hennebont

Throughout the 1341-1342 winter, the House of Montfort supplied, strengthened and reinforced the fort. In April, 1342, when the warm weather had returned, Charles of Blois duly besieged Hennebont castle. Jeanne of Flanders had successfully lifted troop morale over the winter, but when the French army appeared in front of the walls, she felt the need for steeling her army’s resolve.

Until then, she had strutted about, dressed as a duchess. Now, she took up arms, donned armor and personally led the castle’s defense to inspire population and garrison alike. Upping the ante, she personally spoke to the women of the castle, calling on them to “cut their skirts and take their safety into their own hands”. Immediately, they began breaking up the pavements and carried the stones to the battlements to be used as ammunition.

Over the following days and weeks, Jeanne kept a close eye from the castle walls on everything that happened inside the Blois camp. At a certain point during the siege, Jeanne noticed that it was lightly guarded. Most French soldiers happened to be scattered over the nearby woods, foraging. Spotting an opportunity to turn the tide, she gathered 300 cavalrymen and rode out on a great courser. Her force quickly overwhelmed the camp’s defenders, destroyed the tents of Charles of Blois, and torched the place.

This was probably the moment when Jeanne earned the nickname “la Flamme”. However, at least one Frenchman managed to sound the alarm and thousands of soldiers hurried back from the forest to defend their camp. As the fire raged all around, they managed to cut off Jeanne’s retreat route to Hennebont. With a stroke of genius, she turned her force around, left Hennebont for what it was, and retreated to Brest – on the western end of the Breton peninsula.

Charles of Blois immediately gave pursuit, but his larger force on foot could not keep up with Jeanne’s horseback pace. She thus arrived at Brest much earlier than Charles, gathered supplies and around 500 fresh troops, and went back to Hennebont by a different route. The French, to their chagrin, quickly realized what happened and returned to the castle to restart the siege. But Jeanne la Flamme had managed to resupply her army, destroy the enemy’s camp, and – most importantly – scored a crucial moral victory.

**His Majesty’s Naval Service**

Her theatrics thus bought Jeanne crucial weeks of time. But as the powerful French catapults kept hammering away at Hennebont’s walls day after day, the _esprit de corps_ declined again. The initial effects of Jeanne’s antics, impressive as they might have been, faded. Once more locked up inside Hennebont castle, her advisors started to pressure her to surrender by the end of spring. In one of the keep’s upper chambers, a heated discussion erupted, as captain after captain tried to make the steadfast Jeanne change her mind.

Her officers were desperate to the point of rebellion, but when La Flamme looked out the window, a smile appeared on her lips. Ships had appeared on the horizon: the Admiral of the Northern Seas arrived at the head of an English navy. Jeanne would not need to surrender just yet. Evidently, the French had taken up too much time to capture Hennebont and now the window of opportunity had closed. Jeanne la Flamme’s sally and feigned retreat to Brest had undone much of the siege’s progress.

[![Image 4](https://i0.wp.com/thefreelancehistorywriter.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/202112-2_jeanne-at-hennebont_2.jpg?resize=809%2C1044&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/thefreelancehistorywriter.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/202112-2_jeanne-at-hennebont_2.jpg?ssl=1)

_Whilst her captains are desperate to the point of insubordination, Jeanne witnesses the English fleet arriving and knows the tide has turned._

As the ships docked at Hennebont, King Philip’s nightmare had come true: the English landed in Brittany. The War of the Breton Succession had turned into a proxy conflict of the Hundred Years’ War. Overwhelmed by the arrival of the English, the French army lifted the siege and retreated. The tide of the war turned in favor of House Montfort again. But with her husband still in prison and two-thirds of Brittany loyal to her rival Jeanne de Penthièvre, the War of the Two Jeannes was far from over.

Jeanne la Flamme decided she needed more help and went to England herself. King Edward III was a bit preoccupied with hosting feasts and tournaments, but – after a long wait – finally granted Jeanne an audience and promised her further assistance. She set sail back to Brittany with a fine collection of English men-at-arms. However, near Guernsey, they were beset upon by a French fleet that had been lying in ambush. The French grappled the English ships and fierce hand-to-hand combat ensued. Fortunately for the English, Jeanne la Flamme was aboard: she raged across the decks with a glaive and allegedly slew many enemies. By the end of the day, the fight had failed to deliver a clear result and the French retreated. Jeanne and her allies continued towards Brittany.

**Edward, The King**

Around this point in time, the role England began to play in the War of the Breton Succession became a mixed blessing for the Montforts. Although it had been John of Montfort himself, and – after him – Jeanne la Flamme too, who had personally requested reinforcements from king Edward III, the Breton conflict now assumed proportions greater than ever intended. English commanders – not in the least Edward himself – increasingly influenced Breton affairs, relegating Jeanne la Flamme to a background role.

For instance, King Edward landed at Brest and, over the following years, basically took over the Breton conflict. The king enjoyed mixed results in the duchy, however, and a truce was concluded in 1343. Tellingly, the treaty failed to deliver a definitive answer to the underlying question of the Breton succession. At least, the truce allowed John of Montfort to be released from the Louvre prison. Jeanne and John could reunite after two eventful years.

They went to England to make further preparations for continuing their struggle when the truce ran out. When hostilities resumed in 1345, John of Montfort gathered another English army, fought against the French and died – of all places – at Hennebont. Jeanne la Flamme and her infant son were still in England, ready to carry on the succession struggle, but now Edward had had enough. With John of Montfort out of the way, the English king wanted the Breton front for himself. He ordered Jeanne la Flamme to be confined to Tickhill Castle, in northern England.

She was charged with mental illness, although no evidence of that ever surfaced. In essence, Edward used her as a figurehead claimant to augment his own offensive. The king carried Jeanne’s claim in theory, but – in practice – wanted to conduct the war without Montfortist meddling.

**La Flamme’s Legacy**

Over the next two decades, the English steadily gained the upper hand in their Breton theater of war. In the end, Edward allowed Jeanne la Flamme’s (now adult) son John to leave Tickhill and move to Brittany. To further illustrate the balance of power, Edward III instructed him not to marry or wage war – fundamentally, not to do anything – without consulting him first. Perhaps taking after his strong-willed parents, John tried to strike a deal with Charles of Blois anyway by proposing to divide Brittany between them. But the “other” Jeanne, Charles’ wife, would have nothing of it and implored her husband to crush the young Montfort claimant.

Matters quickly came to a head after that. In 1364, an Anglo-Breton force of around 6,000 strong clashed with a French army of roughly 4,000 in strength. Jeanne la Flamme’s son commanded the English center; Charles of Blois the French. Men-at-arms and knights of both sides marched towards each other and, without any maneuvering or tactical tricks, engaged in ferocious and sanguine direct combat. After more than twenty years of war, both armies wanted a decisive result there and then. John, as well as Charles, gave orders not to take any prisoners and to leave as few survivors as possible.

The setup worked, as Charles of Blois was killed in the ensuing melee. His wife Jeanne de Penthièvre tried to carry on his claim like Jeanne la Flamme had done for the Montfortists, but the Blois cause collapsed soon after the battle. The next year, a comprehensive peace treaty was concluded to end the War of the Breton Succession. The son of John of Montfort and Jeanne la Flamme was finally and universally recognized as John IV, Duke of Brittany.

Still locked up in Tickhill Castle, Jeanne la Flamme only learned of these developments sometime later. With her son now wearing the Breton ducal crown, she was of no value to the English king anymore. Edward did not allow Jeanne to leave. Despite having fought so hard for the Montfortist cause, Jeanne la Flamme never set foot in Brittany again. But her efforts were not in vain: she spent the last 10 years of her life – albeit under house arrest – in the knowledge that her son’s rule over the duchy was safe and secure.

Further reading: “The True Chronicles of Jean le Bel, 1290 – 1360” by Jean le Bel (transl. Nigel Bryant); “Joanna of Flanders: Heroine and Exile” by Julie Sarpy; “Women of Medieval France”, Chapter IX, by Pierce Butler; “The Creation of Brittany: A Late Medieval State” by Michael Jones; “Princely Power in Late Medieval France. Jeanne de Penthièvre and the War for Brittany” by Erika Graham-Goering; “The Hundred Years War, Vol 1: Trial by Battle” by Jonathan Sumption.
